With respect, one may also accept the suggestion made by Dr. Zahir that it is necessary to strengthen the Election Commission so that it can conduct the elections fairly and impartially without having to turn to the Care-Taker Government for support. The Election Commission itself may be given the authority to commandeer all necessary assistance and support from the civil administration. It will have at its disposal adequate numbers of members of the civil administration for the purpose of aiding and assisting in the election process. And only these civil administrative personnel will be under the control of the Election Commission. Equally, the services of the disciplined forces may be sought from the President, should it be felt necessary by the Election Commission for proper management of the election process.

1546. Mr. Huq went on to argue that the non- party Care-Taker Government is still 'necessary because the party in power and the main opposition "are not behaving in the proper direction. They are critising each other without respect for other." Well, that takes us back to square one where the Care-Taker Government was created due to the mutual distrust of the opposing political forces. Perhaps, some such sys- tem of neutral interim Government will remain a necessity until the political parties learn to trust each other; at least for the three months necessary for holding general elections. If the Election Commission is given sufficient strength and authority to conduct the elections independently, with all aid and assistance at their command, then it would matter little as to who was heading the Care-Taker Government.

1547. Mr. Huq has suggested that the judiciary should be kept out of the political arena. That is the best way to keep the Judges from being stigmatized due to no fault of their own. But one should reflect upon the need to involve the judiciary at the inception of the Care-Taker Government concept. The judiciary commands high respect now as it did then, when it was felt that only a Judge of the highest judiciary could be trusted to be impartial. This was the feeling of all political parties and hence the whole nation. The feeling persisted during the next two general elections. It was the subsequent alleged calculated manipulation of the retiring age of Supreme Court Judges for political ends that led to the maligning of the system of Care- Taker Government.

1548. Again, going back to the empowered Election Commission, the limelight would be taken away from the head of the Care-Taker Government when the notion is obliterated from the minds of the people that the Care-Taker Government has any function in conducting the electioris. It would be immaterial whether the head of the Care-Taker Government was a retired Chief Justice or any other person of immaculate repute and personality.

1549. With respect, I find good sense in the suggestion from Mr. Huq that the interim government should comprise an equal number of eminent or prominent persons nominated by the opposing political parties. This would give a balanced team who would check each other in their day to day activities during the relatively short period of two and half months when elections are conducted by the Election Commission. Of course, two opposing forces, no matter how mundane their activities would require an 'umpire', especially in the charged atmosphere of suspicion and distrust. Who better to act as 'umpire' than a retired Judge who would have spent his working life on the Bench as an 'umpire'? As I perceive the situation, so long as the 'umpire' realises that the function of the interim government is only to carry out the day to day decisions in relation to running the country and strictly no involvement in the election process, he should be able to deter the other members of his team from delving in or interfering with the activities Of the Election Commission. Of course, that is not to say that an impartial head of the interim government cannot be chosen from civil society. What is important is to ensure political neutrality of the person and his ability to control warring political stalwarts, who might justifiably be suspected of delving into the election process. Allegations of powerful Ministers and politicians visiting local constituencies, even when prohibited by law during the time of election, are not uncommon. It is most essential to allow the Election Commission to maintain the timeframe laid down for the election without let, hindrance or interference from any quarter. That can be achieved only if the Election Commission is given all necessary powers and independence in the conduct of the elections. Mr. Huqgoes on to state that the-non-party Care-Taker Government is not in conformity with the fundamental structure of our Constitution, though he did say earlier that the system was still necessary. He pointed out that the Election Commission in India has been made powerful and independent, and. neutral persons have been selected to form the Election Commission. Our Election Commission has been able to prove its transparency and neutrality in holding the general elections of 2008 and local elections. He suggested that we must have a powerful Election Commission its own budget.

1550. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, on the other hand, firstly submitted that the impugned Amendment does not infringe the Republican character of the State / Constitution. The office of the President still remains to be filled up by the people's representatives and the Constitution retains its Republican character notwithstanding the Thirteenth Amendment. He further sub- mitted that all efforts were made before the Thirteenth Amendment to save democracy and that if it is held invalid, it is almost certain that the opposition parties will not participate in the election and democracy will be a far cry. He added that it is true that the provisions of the Thirteenth Amendment suspend representative government for a short interregnum, but the Amendment ensures operation of democracy in the country. He submitted that there was no alternative to holding election under a Care-Taker government to preserve the democratic character of the Constitution and the country. Democracy has to be suspended for a little while for ultimate survival of democracy. With regard to the independence of the judiciary being affected by the Thirteenth Amendment, he submitted that if a judge passes a judgment for receiving any favour or due to fear of government action, the judge commits breach of his oath; it has nothing to do with the performance of his duty as a judge. By the appointment of a retired Chief Justice or a judge of the Appellate Division the judiciary is not in any way involved.

1551. Mr. TH Khan and Dr. Kamal Hossain, learned Counsel appearing as amici curiae submitted in support of the contention that the Thirteenth Amendment was not illegal or ultra vires the Constitution as there was a national consensus sup- porting electoral reforms to ensure free and fair elections and for that purpose the citizens may make informed choices. They also suggested supplementing the powers of the Election Commission to dis- charge its constitutional mandate. Both learned Counsel were in favour of retention of the system of Care-Taker Government since it was introduced following broad social and political consensus, which was a change brought about by the people to protect their rights to have effective participation in. a free and fair election process. Mr. TH Khan submitted that if Part IXA of the Constitution does not destroy democracy, then Part IIA likewise does not do so.

1552. Mr. M Amirul Islam, learned Counsel appearing as amicus curiae, made submissions in sup- port of the legality of the Amendment, but emphasized the need to have a powerful Election Commission, and above all a correct Electoral Roll. He submitted that in 2006 the Election Commission failed to prepare an up to date voters list and the then President took over the position of Chief Adviser. His action was challenged in the High Court Division, but the Chief Justice stayed the matter.

1553. Mr. Ajmalul Hossain, learned Counsel appearing as amicus' curiae submitted that the Thirteenth Amendment is ultra vires the Constitution as it infringes the democratic nature of the Constitution since Article 7, Part I and Part II contemplate that the country should be governed by elected representatives of the people. Referring to the turn of events in 2006 he suggested that because the political party in opposition did not wish to have an election under the last retired Chief Justice, they took their agitations to the streets and as a result there was a Care-Taker government supported by the army for two years which destroyed the fundamental rights and rule of law.

1554. It must be pointed out that what happened in 2006 was not a consequence of the legality or otherwise of the Thirteenth Amendment, but the failure of the then President to comply with provisions of the Constitution. He did not exhaust the options in Article 58C(3), (4) and (5), before declaring himself the Chief Adviser, which was in fact challenged before the High Court Division, as we note from the submissions of Mr. M Amirui Islam.

1555. Mr. Rokan Uddin Mahrnud, learned Counsel appearing as amicus curiae also submitted in favour of the legality of the Thirteenth Amendment. He referred to the convention whereby after the dissolution of the British Parliament, the outgoing Prime Minister continues until the new Prime Minister takes up his post. But during this interim period he remains unelected. A similar provision exists in our Constitution under Article 58(4). He submitted that if by such provision democracy is not infringed then Article 58B cannot infringe democracy.

1556. Mr. Muhammad Mohsen Rashid, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant made submissions challenging the legality and vires of the Amendment. At the same time he admitted that "the country was coming out of crisis and it made sense to install a Care-Taker Government which could hold free and fair election it was only then that this form of Government aided in installing democracy". He however, gave the example of India thus, "In India the Election Commission was strengthened by a single man, Mr. TN Sasha, This man is individually responsible for changing the face of the Election Commission and today there are more than one billion beneficiaries of such an independent Election Commission. Currently the execution of elections under the Election Commission is such that no one dares to raise a voice or a finger towards that institution whilst having a Care-Taker Government which facilitates the holding of free and fair elections."

1557. The learned Attorney General made submissions in favour of the Amendment pointing out that the Constitution allows non-elected Ministers and Women Members of Parliament who are not elected by the people. He adverted to the necessity of appointment of non-elected persons for the sake of holding free and fair elections. He submitted that the Thirteenth Amendment did not alter the basic structures of the Constitution.

<u>1558. Thus it is seen that the majority of the amici curiae were of the view that the Thirteenth Amendment is not ultra vires the Constitution but many of them were of the view that it cannot survive in the present form. There was general consensus that the Election Commission needs to be given full independence and more power in order that it may hold free and fair elections.</u>

<u>1559. Certainly, the Care-Taker Government system conceived in Bangladesh was quite unique and served its purpose well at the time. The system has been given a bad reputation due to political manipulation. However, a system of interim Government is not unknown and is in operation in many developed and less developed countries of the world. In any democracy there has to be an opportunity for the people to air their views periodically. Hence, elections are held after a stipulated period. Unless the outgoing government holds election during the pendency of its term of office, there will necessarily be a gap between dissolution of Parliament and the sitting of a new Parliament. Any party in power will always wield its might. In the context of our political rivalry, we cannot seriously expect the party in power to abstain from exerting unfair influence during elections. Hence, no fair election can be held while any particular party is still in power. Therefore, there is obvious need for a neutral interim Government. Mr. Huq's suggestion to allow the non-party Care-Taker Government to hold elections is fraught with the same dangers as existed under the Care-Taker Government resulting from the Thirteenth Amendment. What is necessary, with respect, is to totally do away with the notion that the Care-Taker Government is formed to hold elections. A careful reading of the Thirteenth Amendment would expose the fact that the Care-Taker Government is meant only for day to day Government of the country and has no express or implied power to act in relation to the elections, but only to aid and assist the Ejection Commission. With the realisation that the Care-Taker Government or the Chief Adviser of the Care-Taker Government has no power or function with regard to the elections, the need for manipulations and adjustments for that post will be obviated. In. such a situation no aspersions would be cast on the person appointed as the Chief of the neutral interim Government. As for appointment of the head of the interim Government, the suggestion to have the last three Chief Justices to select the Chief Adviser is likely to lead to similar calculative manipulations as in the past. A better solution might be to allow the political parties to suggest five names, excepting ones which have held post in any political party; and any name found common be chosen to head the interim Government.</u>

<u>1560. At this juncture, I would also suggest that the choice of the words "Care-Taker Government" gives the impression of a helpless situation, which may have been apt at the relevant time in 1996 when we needed the "care". However, the term "neutral interim Government" would appear to be apposite for the period in between dissolution of one Parliament, to be replaced by another.</u>

1561. Finally, I would venture to say that in a democratic society no law can be inscribed in stone. Society does not exist in solid state nor in inertia and cannot be expected to go into stagnation. The need for change arises every day intone form or another. Ours is a fragile democracy and the interim period between the dissolution of Parliament and the sitting of the next Parliament is the Achilles heel of that system. In 1996 there was clearly the need for a solution to a political quagmire. The people needed a way out, which they found in the form of the Non-Party Care-Taker Government. The system worked to a great extent for two terms. For reasons which are alluded to above, the system became unworkable. Again, the people must be allowed to decide the solution to the problem. That can only be done through dialogue in Parliament by their ejected representatives. The suggestions made above are mere suggestions. The Supreme Court or the Judges do not make law and it is not their mandate to do so. The Supreme Court has the authority given by the Constitution to declare any law to be ultra vires the Constitution. The Court may travel to the extent of recommending that Parliament should consider enacting a particular legal provision to cater for a given problem which has been brought to its notice, but that does not extend to law-making power.

<u>1562. In conclusion, I find that the Thirteenth Amendment was newither illegal nor ultra vires the Constitution and does not destroy any basic structures of the Constitution. The Republican and Democratic character of the Constitution was no more infringed after the Thirteenth Amendment than it had been before the Non-Party Care-Taker Government system was introduced. However, the system has become unworkable due to the improper exercise of power of the President under Articles 58 C (3), (4), (5) and (6), which led to the unnatural and unconstitutional state of affairs in 2007. In order to avoid' recurrence of such a situation, the mode of setting up of the interim Government, by whatever name it may be called, is to be replaced by another system. It is fully within the power of the people to change the system which will serve them and sustain their democratic rights. It has to be borne in mind and that no system can ever be foolproof. Nevertheless, whatever new system is introduced, it will have to acceptable to the people for it to have durability. As discussed above, the people make their will known by exercising their democratic right through their elected representatives in Parliament.</u>

1563. With the above observations, the appeal is disposed of, without however, any order as to costs.

Order of the Court

1. By majority judgment, the appeal is allowed.

The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set-aside.

2. The Constitution, (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 (Act I of 1996), is ultra vires the Constitution and hereby declared void prospectively.

3. The Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.596 of 2005 is accordingly disposed of.

4. The Government is hereby directed to pay honorarium of Tk.20, 000 to each of the Junior Advocates of the learned amici curiae.

5. There shall be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. M. A. Wahab Miah, with Mr. M. Enayetur Rahim, Advocates ----- for the Petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, A. A. G. ----- for respondent No. 1
parties:
Hafeezuddin Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause why they should not be directed to implement the order passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 45 of 1991 by delivering vacant possession of the building in question, namely, House No. 5/7 Block-D, Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka to the petitioner or such other or further order or orders passed as to this may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts which have given rise to the rule are stated as follows:

The petitioner was alloted House No. 5/7, Block-D Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka by virtue of a registered agreement for allotment of houses executed on 9th February, 1960 and subsequently possession was delivered to him and since that time the petitioner had been in possession of the House in question with his family members-After the liberation of Bangladesh the petitioner was ousted from the House in question by some armed miscreants and since then the same is being occupied by unauthorised persons. The petitioner never left the country nor gave any option for Pakistan. He was an employee of Bangladesh Railway and though he was out of service for some time he resumed his duties on 20.9.1982 and thereafter he retired from service on 1.10.1990. Now he has been drawing his pension as a retired employee of Bangladesh Railway. In spite of giving representations, both orally and in writing to the respondents the concerned Ministry failed to give possession of the house to the petitioner by way of evicting the unauthorised occupant and ultimately the property was Included in the list of abandoned buildings published by the Ministry of Works as per provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The petitioner filed an application before the Court of Settlement under section 7 of the said Ordinance for excluding the house in question from the list of Abandoned Buildings and the said application was registered as Case No. 45/91 (Ka) 180-Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka.

3. The Government contested the said case without filing any written statement denying the material statements made in the application filed in the Court of Settlement. The petitioner having appeared personally before the Court of Settlement, the service book and the service record of. the petitioner having been called for from the Finance Adviser and Chief Accountant (East) of the Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong was duly produced before the Court of Settlement. The Court of Settlement after hearing the learned Advocate of the petitioner as well as the Government lawyer and on perusal of the service Book and other connected records produced by the Railway Authority being satisfied as to the bonafide and genuineness of the petitioner's claim by its judgment and order dated 30th day of September, 1992 allowed the application and excluded the property from the list of abandoned buildings and directed that the petitioner be restored to possession of the house. It was also found by the Court of Settlement that the petitioner was an employee of the Bangladesh Railway and be retired from service in 1990 and now he is a pension holder and the property is not an abandoned property but it was wrongly listed in the 'ka' list.

4. After the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement the petitioner approached the respondents and thereafter filed written application on 5.12.92 to the Minister in-Charge of the Ministry of Works, Secretary, Ministry of Works, Chairman, Abandoned Properties and Management Board requesting them to implement the decision of the Court of Settlement by handing over vacant possession of the house in question to him but no step has yet been taken for giving delivery of possession of the house to the petitioner. The petitioner against filed applications to the Secretary of the Ministry of Works on 20.12.92 and 31.12.92 making similar prayer but to no result. Ultimately the petitioner received a letter issued under the signature of the Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Works that the Ministry has written to the Divisional Commissioner and Chairman of the Abandoned Properties Management Board, Shegun Bagicha for sending the record to the Ministry in respect of the house in question for placing the same before the Writ Committee of the Ministry. Having failed to get delivery of possession of the house in question even after the judgment and order passed in his favour by the Court of Settlement, the petitioner being aggrieved moved this court and, obtained the present rule.

5. Mr. M. A Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the Court of Settlement after due consideration of the evidence and materials on record decided that the property in question was wrongly treated as abandoned and hence directed for the exclusion of the same from the list of the abandoned buildings with a further direction for the restoration of possession of the building to the petitioner but the possession of the property has not yet been restored to the petitioner and in that view of the matter a direction from this court is necessary to be given for restoration of possession of property in question to the petitioner in terms of the judgment and order of the court of Settlement. It is submitted that the Court of Settlement has been constituted by the Government under the provision of section 7 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 and the Government is under legal obligation to, implement, execute the decision given by the said court of settlement and as such for the inaction on the part of the officials of the Government in not implementing/executing the decision passed by the Court of Settlement a mandate from this Hon'ble court seems to be imperative for the implementation and execution of the order of the Court of Settlement.

6. Affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in which the allegations made by the petitioner to the effect that the respondents are not responding with the prayer of the petitioner has been Controverted.

7. Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent no. 1 submitted that the respondents have not expressed their unwillingness to hand over possession of the houses in question to the rightful claimant but the matter is being delayed as a lot of formalities ate to be observed before handing over of the house consequent on the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement. Without appreciating that some time is necessary for the verification of the record and identification of the claimant the petitioner has rushed to this court and hence the learned Assistant Attorney General submitted that the application being pre-mature the petitioner is not entitled to any relief in the same. The learned Assistant Attorney General further submitted that before seeking relief by way of filing the writ application no demand for justice notice was issued and served on the respondents enabling them to take necessary step in the matter. Whatever might be the point raised, the learned Assistant Attorney General found it difficult to justify the in action on the part of the Government in carrying out of the order of the Court of Settlement.

<u>8. From the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement passed on 30th September, 1982 and after hearing both the parties it appears that the learned Court of Settlement after due consideration of the fact and circumstances of the case was clearly of the opinion that the case house is not an abandoned building and it was wrongly included in the list of abandoned building and hence should be excluded from the 'Ka' list. Direction was also been given by the Court of Settlement for the restoration of the possession of the building to the petitioner. The order of the Court of Settlement for restoration of the property in question to the petitioner is final and binding on the respondents in view of section 10 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance 1985, (54 of 1985). Though no specific provision has been made in the Ordinance for the execution of the order of the Court of Settlement, we are of the view that the Government is under legal obligation to give effect to the decision of the Court of Settlement. From the averments made in the affidavit in opposition and the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General it appears that the decision of the court of settlement has not been challenged before any higher forum and that the respondents are not unwilling to give effect of the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement. Since the judgment and order has been passed by the learned Court of Settlement after hearing both the parties it is not desirable that the matter of handing over of the possession of the house in question to the petitioner will be kept in abeyance for an unlimited period. We also do not find sub stance in the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that the writ petition is not maintainable for not issuing demand for justice of notice to the respondents as the authority turned deaf cars to the representations made by the petitioner for obtaining delivery of possession after the judgment and order of the court of settlement.</u>

9. In view of the above, we are of the view that the respondents are required by law to implement the decision of the Court of Settlement and restore the property in question to the petitioner giving effect to the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement.

10. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs. The respondents are directed to restore posse of the property in question to the petitioner within 60 days from the date of receipt of the order.

End.

lawyer:
Shasti Sarker, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
MA Halim, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abul Hossain and others ------ Petitioners 
vs 
Habibullah Mia & ors ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: The revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 20-5-2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 9-7-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, dismissing the suit.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 116 of 1993 against the defendants for declaration of title and for permanent injunction in respect of 0.62 acres of land in plot No. 36 within mouza Mandail under Keranigonj Police Station.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the suit land was owned by Zaminder Kalinarayan Roy, who awarded Sikkim taluk of the land to his son Babu Dakhinacharan Roy; that one Haji Gandu Kha Bepari, son of Paltan Kha took possession of the Sikkim taluk and transferred the possessory right of the land in favour of his two sons Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Alek, that Haji Gandhu Kha Bepari excavated pond on the suit plot No. 36 in the year of 1320 and was in possession of the pond and he also cultivated fish and used the water of the pond. It is further stated that the residential house of Gandhu Kha Bepari was just beside the suit pond in plot No. 34; that Gandhu Kha Bepari left behind his two sons Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Alek and 5 daughters and that the land of the pond was taken in the names of his two sons and his other heirs did not receive any inheritance in the property.

4. Their further case is that Haji Mia Kha was the brother of Haji Gandhu Kha who was the eldest person in his family and started looking after all the properties of the family; that CS record accordingly, was collusively prepared in the name of Haji Mia Kha alone but still Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Alek remained in possession of the suit land and that Haji Mia Kha never claimed any independent title in the suit pond. It is further stated that Abdul Khaleque died in the year 1968 leaving behind one son Abdul Mannan, plaintiff No. 8, and 3(three) daughters namely, plaintiffs Nos. 9 to 11. Alek died in the year 1948 leaving behind son Hanif, predecessor of defendants Nos. 1 to 8, son Abul Hossain, plaintiff No. 1, son Motiur Rahman plaintiff No. 2 and son Shahabuddin, predecessors of plaintiff Nos. 4 to 7 and daughter Afia Khatoon, plaintiff No. 3 and that subsequently, during SA operation, the suit pond was wrongly recorded in the names of the defendants Nos. 9 and 10, Abdul Majid Kha and Monnaf Kha, sons, Mariam Bibi who was daughter of Haji Gandu Kha Bepari and in the name of Abdul Rashid Kha, father of defendants Nos. 11 and 12 but they did not enjoy the suit pond during the life-time of Hanif, that Hanif on their behalf possessed the suit pond. That all the rent receipts and documents were under the possession of Md Hanif and that Md Hanif during his lifetime did not claim the independent title or possession in the suit pond till his death in 1989.

5. Plaintiff's further case is that on 1-1-1993 the defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 claimed the independent title in the suit pond on the basis of purchase of the same by their father Md Hanif and restrained the plaintiffs from using the water of the pond and claimed the yearly sale proceed of the fish. Then defendant Nos. 1 to 8 disclosed that SA Khatian and mutation were exclusively prepared in the name of their father Md Hanif. On enquiry it was revealed that said mutation case was a forged one; that the defendant had no independent title and possession in the suit pond. On the other hand, the defendant Nos. 9 to 12 acquired title in the suit pond by virtue of adverse possession. Aa the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 claimed independent title in the suit pond and also restrained the plaintiffs from enjoying usufruct of the pond, hence plaintiffs are constrained to file the suit.

6. Defendant Nos. 1 to 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement alleging, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable, that the payment of the court fee is not proper and that there is no cause of action of the suit. It is further stated that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit pond; that Haji Gandu Kha and Haji Mia Kha were not brothers as their fathers are different, and that Haji Mia Kha was the son of Pagan Bepari and Gandhu Kha was the son of Haji Ashrafuddin. Defendants' further contention is that CS record was correctly prepared in the name of Haji Mia Kha and that on the death of Haji Mia Kha, his heirs executed and registered solenama on 27-8-1916 and according to the terms of solenama the suit pond fell into the saham of his son Md Yasin Khan; that Yasin Khan left Abdul Mazid Kha, Abdul. Mannaf Kha, Abdur Rashid Kha and two daughters Kamrunnessa and Amirunnessa and a wife Mariam Bibi, that other heirs died leaving sons and daughters who acquired the permanent marashi title under the sikim taluk of Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Alek; that all the interests were extinguished after the acquisition of Zamindari system and SA record was prepared correctly in the name of Abdul Mazid and Abdul Mannaf, son of Yasin Kha, Nazir Ahmed Kha and Abdul Hamid, sons of Abdul Rashid in equal share. It is further stated that the father of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 Md Hanif purchased the suit pond on 29-5-1973 by registered deed No. 13424 from Abdul Mannaf Khan, Nazir Ahmed Khan and Abdul Hamid Khan and later on 16-4-1980 purchased also the share of Abdul Majid Kha through registered deed No. 8112 dated 16-4-1980 and that the defendants Nos. 1 to 8 have been possessing the suit pond by paying the rents in the name of their father Md Hanif Miah who mutated his name in SA khatian. It is further stated that plaintiff brought the suit on false claims upon the suit pond as they never possessed the suit pond nor did they acquire title in suit pond, that Gandhu Kha had no title in the suit pond and thus the plaintiffs received nothing from him. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. The plaintiffs adduced 5 witnesses and defendant adduced 5 witnesses and both the parties exhibited some documents in the trial Court in support of their respective claim.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 9-7-2000 holding, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable as they brought the suit having no power on behalf of other plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit pond.

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 9-7-2002, the plaintiffs filed title appeal in the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka and on transfer the appeal was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, in charge of 5th Court, Dhaka, who by his judgment and decree dated 20-5-2002 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree dated 9-7-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Suit No. 116 of 1993.

10. The point for determination is, whether the learned. Additional District Judge committed any error of law in his judgment and decree dated 9-7-2002 occasioning failure of justice.

11. Mr Shasti Sarker, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court erred in law, fact and equity in misreading of the evidence on record and in misappreciating, particularly, evidence of PWs 4 and 5 thereby arrived at wrong conclusion that the brotherhood of Haji Gandu Kha Bepari and Haji Mia Kha was not proved. He further submits that the learned Court below erred in law and facts in misconstruing the evidence on record in asmuch as, the plaintiff by adducing witnesses PW 1 to PW 5 clearly proved the plaint case; that the suit pond was the ejmali property of plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 as the successors of Haji Miah Kha; that the record of the suit pond in the name of Haji Mia Kha in CS, SA and RS khatian was clearly wrong and that the learned Courts below committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

12. Mr MA Halim, the learned Advocate for the defendants-respondents-opposite parties, submits that the plaintiffs-petitioners have no right, title and possession in the suit pond; that Haji Ghandu Khan Bepari and Haji Miah Kha were not brothers of each other; that the CS record in the name of Haji Mia Kha was correctly prepared; that on the death of Haji Mia Kha his heirs executed a registered solenama on 27-8-1916 and on the basis of the solenama suit pond fell in the saharn of his son Md Yasin Khan, that Md Yasin Khan died leaving behind Abdul Mazid Kha, Abdul Mannaf Kha, Abdur Rashid Kha; that the father of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 Md Hanif purchased the suit pond on 29-5-1973 by registered deed No. 13424 from Abdul Mannaf Khan, Nazir Ahmed Khan and Abdul Hamid Khan and later on 16-4-1980 also purchased the share of Abdul Mazid Kha through registered deed No. 8112 dated 16-4-1980 and that the name of Md Hanif was mutated; that defendant Nos. 1 to 8 have been possessing the suit pond by paying rents and that the plaintiffs brought the suit on false claims and they have no title and possession of the suit land.

13. In the face of arguments advanced by the learned Advocates of contending parties, it is necessary for us to scrutinise the material evidence on record to come to a proper decision in this case.

14. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has placed before us the plaint, the written statement, the evidence of witnesses examined by the contending parties, the material exhibits as well as the impugned judgments.

15. It is not disputed that the suit pond measuring 0.62 acres appertaining to CS plot No. 36 of CS Khatian No. 13 under Mandail Mouza of Keranigonj PS in the District of Dhaka. There is no denying of the fact that CS Khatian No. 13 was recorded in the name of Haji Mia Kha, son of Late Palton Kha Bepari, that SA record was prepared in the name of Majid Kha and Abdul Mannaf Kha, son of Md Yasin Kha, Nazir Ahmed Kha and Abdul Hamid, son of Abdul Rashid and that the suit plot was mutated in the name of Md Hanif Miah, son of late Abdul Malek Miah and who also paid rent to the government.

16. The case of the plaintiffs is that Hazi Gandu Kha took lease of 0.62 acres of land from suit plot in 1310 in the names of his 2(two) sons namely, Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Malek, but there is no document in support of their contention and no record was prepared on the basis of alleged settlement. It transpires that CS record was prepared in the name of Haji Mia Kha. Thereafter, the plaintiff has taken different view that Haji Gandu Khan and Miah Kha are full brothers and that Haji Mia Kha being eldest brother collusively prepared CS record in his name, in spite of such wrong record the heirs of Gandu Kha have been retaining title and possession in the suit pond and that on 1-1-1993 when defendant Nos. 1 to 8 in collusion with defendant No. 14 threatened the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs, then they filed suit for declaration in respect of the suit pond and for permanent injunction restraining defendant Nos. 1 to 12 from enjoying the suit pond and for declaring the SA. Khatian fraudulent and collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

17. The defence case, on the other hand, is that Haji Mia Kha, son of Palton Kha, had been possessing the suit pond by virtue of Settlement and thus CS khatian was correctly prepared in his name which is marked Exhibit 'Ka'. Haji Mia Kha transferred the suit plot to some of his heirs by different Heba Deeds but subsequently, dispute arose among the heirs of Haji Mia Kha which was resolved by a registered sole-deed dated 27-8-1996 which is marked Exhibit 'X' and as per the terms of solenama the suit plot was devolved upon Yasin Kha who died leaving 4 (four) sons namely, Mojid Kha, Abdul Mannan Kha, Abdur Rashid Kha and Roshid and 2 (two) daughters named Kameronnessa and Ameronnessa and widow Moriom Bibi. After the death of Morion Bibi, Ameronnessa and Rashid Kha, Majid Kha and Monnaf Kha, sons of Yasin, Nazir Ahmed Kha and Hamid Kha, son of Rashid Kha got the suit land by way of inheritance and by virtue of registered kabala deed dated 7-5-1973 marked exhibit 'Gha' and thus the SA record was prepared in the names of Abdul Majid Kha, Abdul Mannaf Kha, Nazir Ahmed Kha and Abdul Hamid Kha in equal share and SA record is marked exhibit Ka(1). It transpires that Abdul Majid and others paid rent to the government by rent receipts marked exhibit 'Ga' and it further transpires that father of defendant Nos. 1 to 8 Md Hanif purchased the suit pond from Mannaf Kha, Nazir Ahmed Kha, Abdul Rashid Kha and Abdul Hamid Kha by virtue of Kabala deed No. 13424 executed on 7-5-1973 marked exhibit 'Gha' and Md Hanif Miah also purchased the share of Abdul Mazid Kha by a registered Kabala No. 8112. Thus, Md Hanif Miah acquiring title of the suit land had been possessing suit land paying rent to the government by a rent receipt marked exhibit 'Ga'/1 and RS Khatian is marked Exhibit Ka /2 was prepared in his name and his name was mutated and the mutation khatian is marked exhibit 'kha'. After the death of Md Hanif Miah, his heirs, defendant Nos. 1 to 8, have been possessing the suit pond.

18. The plaintiffs failing to establish their title in the suit pond, tried to take another plea that Haji Gandu Kha Bepari, predecessors of the plaintiffs, was the brother of Haji Miah Kha who being elder brother and Karojokarok of Haji Gandu Kha Bepari illegally managed to prepare CS record in his name depriving Haji Gandu Bepari and thus the plaintiffs claim title in the suit pond by inheritance.

19. The defendant Nos. 1 to 8 vehemently opposed such assertion of the plaintiffs. The defence case is that Haji Mia Kha was the son of Late Palton Kha of village Amirabagh, whereas Haji Gandu Kha was the son of Late Ashraf Bepari of village Kusiararbagh.

20. CS Khatian proves that father's name of Haji Miah Kha was Paltan Kha but plaintiffs without filing any document failed to prove that Gandu Kha's father's name was also Paltan Kha. The plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 admitted in his evidence that Mia Kha hails from village Amirabagh and that the village of Gandu Kha is at Kusiarbagh. PW 2 Basu Mia knows nothing about the relationship of Gandu Mia Kha and Miah Kha. PW 5 deposed that he has no document to show that Haji Gandu Kha and Mia Kha are full brothers. PW 3 Ishaque Mia deposed nothing on this point. PW 4 Aynal Hoque deposed that he has nothing to show that Gandhu Kha and Miah Kha are brothers.

21. On the other hand, defendant No. 3 as DW 1 deposed that there was no relationship between Hazi Gandu Kha and Haji Mia Kha, DW 2 Md Yakob categorically deposed that Haji Mia Kha was son of Paltan Kha whereas Gandu Kha was the son of Ashraf Bepari.

22. The plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners filed suit for declaration of title and for permanent injunction. In such case burden of proof lies on the person who desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right. Section 101 of the Evidence Act runs thus:

"Whoever desires any court to give judgment as of any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist. When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person."

<u>23. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it. It is reasonable and just that the suitor who relies upon the existence of a fact should be called upon to prove his own case. The party on whom the onus of proof lies must, in order to succeed, establish the case. He cannot, on failure to do so, take advantage of the weakness of his adversary's case. He must succeed by the strength of his own right and the clearness of his own proof. The burden of proving the case is upon the claimant.</u>

24. In the instant case, the plaintiffs claim their title on two counts, firstly, they claim that Haji Gandu Kha took lease of 0.62 acres of land in the names of his sons Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Alek and the subsequent heirs of Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Malek, who are plaintiffs, claim the suit land by virtue of lease. But the plaintiffs have totally failed to file any documents of lessee or any records of the alleged lease and secondly, the plaintiffs claim that Gandu Kha was the full brother of recorded tenant Haji Mia Kha and thus the successors of Gandu Kha who are plaintiffs, acquired the suit land by inheritance and thus they are in joint possession of the successors of Mia Kha. The brotherly relationship of Gandu Kha and Mia Kha has not been proved nor has been proved any benami transaction by Mia Kha and thus successors plaintiffs of Gandu Kha acquired nothing from Mia Kha and their possession in the suit land has not also been proved.

<u>25. Since the plaintiffs have failed to prove the title and possession in the suit land, as such, their prayer for injunction does not lie. We find support of this view by the rulings reported in 14 DLR 44 and 22 DLR 385.</u>

<u>26. Section 110 of the Evidence Act gives effect to the principle that possession is prima facie evidence of complete title; anyone who intends to oust the possessor must establish a right to do so. This is to be presumed from lawful possession until the want of title or a better title is proved. Possession is prima facie proof of ownership, possession has a two-fold value; it is the evidence of ownership, and is itself the foundation of a right to possession.</u>

<u>27. In the instant case, the plaintiffs claim title along with the contesting defendants and such assertion of the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land have not at all been proved. On the other hand, the title and possession of the contesting defendants on the basis of valid deed has been proved. The defendants possession in the suit land has strengthened the title of the defendants in the suit land.</u>

28. By section 101 of the Evidence Act, the plaintiff has to prove the whole of the facts which he alleges to entitle him to judgment.

29. But section 103 of the Evidence Act states that "The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on that person who wishes the court to believe in its existence, unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person." when the defendant alleges that he has right, title and interest in the suit property which the plaintiff does not accept. In such circumstances it be Comes a fact which is asserted by the defendant and is denied by the plaintiff. As per section 103 of the Evidence Act, the onus of proving the same is on the defendant. Whenever a person asserts affirmatively as part of his case that a certain state of things is present or is absent, or that a particular thing is insufficient for a particular purpose, that is an averment which he is bound to prove affirmatively.

<u>30. Here, in this case, the plaintiffs claim the suit pond firstly by way of lease and alternatively by inheritance showing Gandu Kha as full brother of Mia Kha and both the assertions of the plaintiffs have been proved false. When the assertions of the plaintiffs have not been proved, than as per provision of section 103 of the Evidence Act, the burden rebuts to the defendants. Then we have to see how far the assertions of defendants have been proved. It appears from the evidence on record that the predecessors of the defendant Haji Mia Kha claimed title in suit pond by way of settlement and accordingly, CS record was prepared in the name of Mia Kha, that the heirs of Mia Kha transferred the suit pond to Abdul Mannaf Kha and others and on the basis of this sale deed, SA record was prepared in the name of Abdul Mannaf, Abdul Majid, Nazir Ahmed and Abdul Hamid and the Khatian market Exhibit Ka(1) who also paid rent through rent receipt marked Exhibit 'Ga'. It further transpires from evidence that Abdul Mannaf and others having right, title, interest and possession in the suit pond transferred the same in favour of Md Hanif Mia by a kabala deed No. 13424 dated 7-5-1993 marked exhibit-Gha who also mutated his name through mutation khatian marked Exhibit Kha(2) and Hanif Miah also paid rent by rent receipt marked Exhibit Ga(1). Thus the assertion of the defendants to the effect that they have title and possession in the suit pond has been proved.</u>

31. It is well settled principle of law that the plaintiff is to prove its case which the plaintiffs of this case have totally failed. On the other hand, the defendants have proved their assertion.

32. A plaintiff in order to get declaration in respect of any land, he must have 'legal character' to institute the suit against any person and such character is envisaged in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act runs thus:

"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may, in its discretion, make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.

Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so."

33. The object of this section is merely to perpetuate and strengthen testimony regarding title of the plaintiff so that adverse attacks on it may not weaken it. This section does not sanction any and every kind of declaration but only a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to a specific legal character or to any right as to property.

34. Legal character has been taken to mean legal status. Legal character is meant status or the position which a person occupies in the eye of law. Duties and functions of the courts are to decide disputes between parties in accordance with law.

35. The relief claimed under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is, no doubt, discretionary, but the real test for its application is, whether the plaintiff recalling apprehends that an interested person may deny the plaintiff's title. The jurisdiction to give a declaratory judgment should be exercised sparingly with great care and with extreme caution. The relief being discretionary no person can claim declaration as of right. The court has discretion to grant it or not on consideration of all circumstances of the case and evidence on record. Though the grant of a declaratory relief is entirely at the discretion of the court, the discretion has to be exercised on certain well recognised principles. That is the plaintiff has to prove its case to the hilt and a declaration cannot be given whose conduct is fraudulent. Where a declaratory decree has been given by the trial Court, the appellate Court or the Court of revision should not interfere unless it is satisfied that the lower Court acted in an arbitrary or perverse manner. These courts would however, not intervene when the Court of first instance had soundly exercised its discretion.

<u>36. In the instant case, on perusal of the evidence on record, it appears the plaintiffs have totally failed to prove their case by oral and documentary evidence. Their contention of lease has no legs to stand which is totally false. Moreover, the plaintiffs have not come to the court with clean hands to get a discretionary relief as the plaintiffs tried to show his predecessor Gandu Kha as the brother of Mia Kha which has been proved false and fraudulent. Sections 42 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act deal respectively with suits for declaration and injunction, both being discretionary and equitable reliefs which the plaintiffs of this case have sought for. The principle laid down in section 56(J) rests on the maximum that he who seeks equity must do equity and should come with clean hands. In this case, the plaintiffs have totally failed to prove their case. Moreover, they have not come to the court with clean hands, so they cannot get equity.</u>

37. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 9-7-2000. On appeal, the learned Additional District Judge also dismissed the appeal by the judgment dated 20-5-2002 affirming the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge. The learned Subordinate Judge framing the issues elaborately discussed each point separately giving reasons thereon and his judgment does not suffer any legal infirmity, rather his judgment is self-contained and well-reasoned. The learned Additional District Judge passed his judgment disclosing the points of determination on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. Our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Matin Choudhury vs Chapala Rani Sen and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 205 held that concurrent findings of facts by the trial Court and the first appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which has affected the merit of the case. We find that the judgment of the trial Court as well as of the appellate Court committed no error of law or of principle which has not affected the merit of the case and the judgment of the trial Court as well as of the appellate Court deserve consideration.

39. In view of what we have discussed and considered above, we are of the opinion that the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka committed no error of law in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

40. We, therefore, find no merit in the revision which fails accordingly.

41. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree affirming the judgment of the trial Court are upheld.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

lawyer:
Morshed Ahmed Khan, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Sayeda Afsar Jahan, Deputy Attorney-General—For the Respondents.
parties:
Mahbubul Haque Sikder ------ Petitioners 
vs 
Commissioner of Customs & others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J: The petitioner obtained the instant Rule calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 14-6-1998, 25-6-1998 and 28-6-1998 issued by the respondent No. 1 imposing 150% supplementary duty as per Finance Act, 1998 (Annexure A) on the importation of Volvo Cars by the petitioners should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents should not be directed to calculate the duties and taxes in respect of the said imported vehicles of the petitioners as per Finance Act, 1997 imposing such tax @ 60%.

2. It has been asserted in the writ petition that the petitioner, being the partner of Messrs Al Traders, is the sole agent in Bangladesh for the world famous 'Volvo Cars' made in Sweden. The petitioner's firm has been duly registered with the office of the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports as importer and obtained Import Registration No. Ba. 51472 on 13-10-1997. The petitioner in course of their business established a letter of credit No. 01-261-97 on 15-10-1997 through Prime Bank Limited, Motijheel Branch, Dhaka in favour of Messrs Volvo Car International for importation of 15 Units Volvo Cars from Sweden for an amount of US$ 3,94,500. The supplier Messrs Volvo Car International pursuant to the said letter of credit supplied 12 units Volvo Cars by three consignments. The first consignment of 6 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the vessel MV Sovereign Maersk on 21-11-1997 and six bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035617, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035737, and GOT035739 all dated 21-11-1997 were issued. The second consignment of 2 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the Vessel MV Knud Maersk on 28-11-1997 and two bills of lading Nos. GOT035374 and GOT035805 all dated 28-11-1997 were issued. The third consignment of 4 units Volvo Cars were shipped on board of the Vessel MV Kristen Mearsk on 5-12-1997 and four bills of lading Nos. GOT035727, GOT036043, GOT036044 and GOT036050 all dated 5-12-1997 were issued. All those consignments were loaded from the port of Gothenburg, Sweden with destination to Chittagong and the place of delivery was ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka. These three consignments reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka within the month of December, 1997 and January, 1998. The petitioners through their clearing agent Messrs Azad Traders submitted bills of entries along with relevant documents in order to release six units Volvo cars out of 12 units Volvo Cars. The petitioners paid 42.5% customs duty, 60% supplementary duty, 15% VAT, AIT 2.5% L Fees and 2.5% IDSC and released those six units of Volvo Cars on 19-1-1998, 26-10-1998, 1-6-1998, 25-6-1998 covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035739, GOT035727 and GOT036044 respectively.

3. The further case of the petitioners is that they could not obtain release of the remaining cars expeditiously as the Customs Authority had asked for manufacturer's price and other information and the petitioner has to spend time for collection of those documents and information to satisfy the queries of the Customs Authority. Subsequently, the petitioners on 16-6-1998 through their clearing agent Messrs Azad Traders submitted further six bills of entry Nos. 06891, 06892, 06893, 06895 and 06896 along with relevant documents to release the remaining six units of Volvo Cars covered under the bills of lading Nos. GOT035637, GOT035617, GOT036043, GOT036050, GOT035374 and GOT035805. But the respondents, Customs Authority, calculated the duties and taxes along with 150% supplementary duty as per Finance Act, 1998 instead of 60% of such as per the Finance Act, 1997 although the bills of entry were submitted long before the Finance Act, 1998 came into effect. The petitioner challenging such imposition of enhanced supplementary duty as per the Finance Act, 1998 preferred this writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi.

4. The Rule is duly served upon the respondents and the learned Deputy Attorney-General, Ms Sayeda Afsar Jahan appeared on behalf of the respondents but did not prefer any affidavit-in-opposition.

5. The learned Advocate Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, appearing for the petitioner, after taking us through the various Annexures appended to the writ petition, submits that the petitioner imported altogether 12 units Volvo Cars under the same letter of credit through three consignments which reached ICD, Kamalapur in the month of December, 1997 and January, 1998 out of which the petitioner released six units of Volvo Cars by submitting different bills of entry. But subsequently, when the petitioner attempted to release the remaining six units Volvo Cars and filed the bills of entry in time, the respondent, with an ulterior motive, did not receive the bills of entry for the remaining cars till budget for 1998 was tabled in the parliament and till the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act was amended to include the enhanced rate of supplementary duty upon the importation of those cars by the petitioner. Mr Ahmed categorically submits that although the petitioner through his C&F agent attempted to submit the bills of entry as soon as the consignment reached the ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, the respondents did not register the same till 16-6-1998. The learned Advocate in support of his contention has taken us to the dates of shipment of the consignments and its arrival at ICD, Kamlapur and concluded that if the respondents were not driven by an ulterior motive, the petitioner could effect release of the entire goods much earlier than, the imposition of enhanced rate of supplementary duty on the importation of the cars by the petitioner Mr Ahmed, finally, submits that the petitioner had been forced to undergo financial prejudice by the respondents for which his right to be treated in accordance with law has been violated for which the petitioner is entitled to the relief as prayed for.

6. On the other hand, the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mrs Sayeda Afsar Jahan, advanced argument against the contentions of the petitioner regarding an ulterior motive and submits that the petitioner failed to substantiate his grounds of objection by any cogent and material documents for which the petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for.

7. We have heard the learned Advocate, perused the writ petition and the Annexures appended thereto. We have also examined the relevant law and the SRO, the bills of entry submitted by the petitioner and also perused the Customs file which was called for by this Court to ascertain the actual date of submission of the bills of entry to the Customs Authority. We have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar.

8. The petitioner mainly contends, that although the three consignments containing 12 units Volvo Cars had been reached much earlier than the enhancement of the supplementary duty by the Finance Act, 1998 and the collection of it by the effect of Provisional Collection of Taxes Act from 1st June, 1998, yet the respondents with an ulterior motive to collect more duties from the petitioner has dragged the receiving of bills of entry from the petitioner to a date when the budget for 1998 was tabled in the Parliament proposing enhanced rate of supplementary duty. To appreciate this contention, it is required to examine the exact date of filing of bills of entry for which this Court called for the relevant Customs Nothi and accordingly, the same has been perused by this Court.

9. Admittedly, in the month of January, 1998 there was no system for electronic filing of bill of entry for which the filing date of bill of entry has to be ascertained from the receiving seal affixed at the bill of entry. It appears that affixing of this receiving seal in the body of the bill of entry is the exercise of the respondents Customs Authority and the person who is submitting the bill of entry had no weapon to compel the Customs Authority to affix the receiving seal immediately at its submission and there appears to exist a scope to delay in affixing this receiving seal on the body of the document in accordance with the sweet will of the receiving authority. Mr Ahmed, vigorously argued that the C&F agent of the petitioner attempted to submit the bill of entry for the remaining six units of Volvo Cars in the month of January, 1998 as soon as the consignments reached ICD, Kamalapur but the respondents primarily, on the ground of insufficient documents and thereafter, on an ulterior motive, did not receive the same till 16-6-1998.

10. It appears from the Annexure C, which is the letter of credit No. 01-261-97 opened through Prime Bank Limited, Moulvibazar Branch, Dhaka, that the petitioner under the said letter of credit proposed to import altogether 15 units of Volvo $ 90 Sweden Car of different colours and the same were shipped from Gothenburg, Sweden through the shipping company Maersk Line. The supplier Messrs Volvo Car International Limited supplied 12 units Volvo cars through three consignments. From Annexure D, it appears that the first consignment containing six units of Volvo Cars was shipment on board the vessel MV Sovereign Maersk on 21-11-1997 and six bills of lading being Nos. GOT035615, GOT035617, GOT035619, GOT035734, GOT035737, and GOT035739 all dated 21-11-1997 were issued. This first consignment reached ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka on 31-12-1997 and the petitioner effected release of four units of Volvo Cars of the first consignment covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734 and GOT035739 dated 19-1-1998 out of total six unit cars. The second consignment containing two units Volvo Cars, was shipped on board the vessel MV Knud Maersk on 28-11-1997 and two bills of lading being No. GOT035374 and GOT035805 both dated 28-11-1997 were issued which reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, in the month of January, 1998 but the petitioner did not take release of the cars of this 2nd consignment. The third consignment containing four units Volvo Cars was shipped on board the vessel MV Kristen Maersk on 5-12-1997 and four bills of entry Nos. GOT035727, GOT036043, GOT036044 and GOT036050 all dated 5-12-1997 were issued which reached ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka, on 18-1-1998. The petitioner effected release of two cars out of 3rd consignment covered under the bills of lading No. GOT035727 and GOT036044 but did not effect release of remaining six units Volvo Cars two from 1st consignment, total two of the 2nd consignment and two from 3rd consignment. The contention of the petitioner is that he could not effect the release of the remaining six units Volvo Cars due to the non-receipt of bills of entry by the Customs Authority till 16-6-1998, and such, non-receipt of bills of entry is evident from the fact that the respondents did not take step under section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969 in respect of putting the cars on sale through auction after the laps of statutory period to effect release of consignment.

11. We do not find any substance in the contention of the petitioner mainly for two reasons.

12. Firstly, the petitioner contends that he could not effect release of six units Volvo Cars due to non-receipt of bills of entry by the respondents till 16-6-1998 though the same was submitted much earlier and the respondents with an ulterior motive wanted some superfluous documents which compelled the petitioner to collect the same at the cost of time. This contention appears to be devoid of any basis, since the petitioner effected release of four units Volvo Cars from the 1st and two units of Volvo Cars from the 3rd consignment of the same make, same engine and some model. If the petitioner could effect release of six units of Volvo Cars out of ten units Volvo Cars of two consignments of the same particulars then, the story of asking for some superfluous documents of the same class cars does not hold any water.

13. The learned Deputy Attorney-General strenuously argued that the petitioner did not voluntarily take release of the six units Volvo Cars due to his miscalculated aspiration that ensuing budget will reduce the duty on import of cars but when to his prejudice the rate of supplementary duty has been enhanced, the petitioner invented the story of non-receipt of bills of entry in time and now comes up with a fictitious story of malafide through the supplementary affidavit about which not an iota of fact is mentioned in the original writ petition.

14. We find substance in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General as it appears from the relevant Customs Nothi, which this Court called for, that the petitioner submitted the bills of entry for releasing the four units Volvo Cars from the 1st consignment on 18-1-1998 covered by bills of lading Nos. GOT035615, GOT035619, GOT035734 and GOT035739 and the same was released on 19-1-1998, 19-1-1998, 19-1-1998 and 26-1-1998 respectively after observing all the legal formalities. Thereafter, the petitioner submitted bills of entry for releasing two units Volvo Cars from the 3rd consignment on 29-4-1998 covered by bills of lading No. GOT035727 and GOT036044 and the same was released on 1-6-1998 and 25-6-1998 respectively. There-after, the petitioner submitted bill of entry for effecting release of two units Volvo Car from 1st consignment, all the two units Volvo Cars of 2nd consignment and two units Volvo Cars from 3rd consignments on 16-6-1998 when the rate of supplementary duty has been enhanced to @ 150% by the provision of Finance Act, 1998 and the same became leviable through the operation of Provisional Collection of Taxes Act from 1st June, 1998. Nothing appears from the Customs Nothi that any additional documents were asked from the petitioner or that the petitioner ever submitted any additional documents with his submission of bills of entry allegedly much earlier than 16-6-1998. Thereafter, we do not find any reason to treat these subsequent bills of entry as post-dated made by the respondents with an ulterior motive to collect duties at higher rates.

15. Secondly, from the Customs Nothi, we find that the Customs Authority on receiving the bills of entry on 16-6-1998 assessed the Customs Duty on 28-6-1998 and the petitioner obtained Rule Nisi on 25-8-1998 which was served upon the respondents on 7-9-1998. Thereafter, all the steps in the said Customs Nothi was stopped due to the pendency of the Rule. It further appears that petitioner after getting interim order in this Rule has taken release of only two units Volvo Cars as per the interim order of this Court and did not take release of remaining four units Volvo Cars in spite of the indulgence given by this Court to effect release of remaining six units Volvo Cars after furnishing appropriate Bank guarantee. The respondents although once took step to auction the said four units Volvo Cars under provision of section 82 of the Customs Act but considering the pendency of the instant Rule did not auction those cars which still remain with the Customs Custody.

16. Therefore, we do not find any substance in the contention of the petitioner that the Customs Authority having been empowered to take step under section 82 of the Customs Act, since failed to exercise such power, the same should not be treated in favour of the contention that the bills of entry were submitted by the petitioner much earlier than is showed by the Customs Authority as on 16-6-1998.

17. From section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969, we do not find that the same is non-relaxable provision so as to put the consignment on auction just after 45 days of its delivery in the Customs custody. Section 82 of the Customs Act runs as follows:

"82. Procedure in case of goods not cleared or warehoused or transhipped after unloading within a specified period—(1) If any goods are not entered and cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within forty-five days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs port or a land customs station, or within thirty days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs airport, or within such extended period as the appropriate officer may allow, such goods may, after due notice given to the owner, if his address could be ascertained or published in the newspaper, if his address could not be ascertained, be sold under the orders of the appropriate officer:

Provided that—

(a) animals and perishable and hazardous goods may, with the permission of the appropriate officer, be sold at any time;

(b) arms, ammunition or military stores may be sold or otherwise disposed of at such time and place and in such manner as the Board may, with the approval of the Government, direct."

Provided further that nothing in this section shall authorise removal for home consumption of any dutiable goods without payment of customs duties thereon.

(2) Where any goods are sold under sub-section (1) pending adjudication, appeal, revision or decision of a Court, the proceeds of such sale shall be deposited into the Government treasury and if, on such adjudication or in such appeal or revision, it is found or if the Court S finds that the goods so sold are not liable to confiscation the proceeds of the sale shall after necessary deduction of duties, taxes or dues as provided in section 201, be refunded to the owner.

<u>18. From bare reading of the section this Court has no hesitation to hold that the provision made therein regarding putting the imported consignment on auction due to failure of the importer to effect release of the goods within 45 days is relaxable provision as the time barrier may be extended by the appropriate officer of the Customs Authority. Therefore, we do not find any reason to rely on the analogy made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner to show that failure to put the consignment on auction by the Customs Authority just after 45 days, ipso facto, proves that the bills of entry was submitted much earlier than the date it shows on the body of bills of entry.</u>

<u>19. On the facts and circumstances of the case, we find that the petitioner submitted the bill of entry for effecting release of six units of Volvo Cars on 16-6-1998 and, therefore, liable to pay the duties and taxes prevailing on the said date and accordingly, the assessment made in the relevant Customs Nothi was made in accordance with law.</u>

20. Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, in substantiating his contention that his vested right as to the rate of duty prevailing at the date when he opened the letter of credit cited the decision of the case of Cab Express (BD) Limited vs Commissioner of Customs and Nipun Cab Limited vs Commissioner of Customs reported in 9 BLC 398 in which one of us is the author Judge, we find that the facts of that case is quite distinguishable from the instant case and, as such, the principle enunciated in that case as to the vested right has no manner of application in this case.

21. On the discussion and reasoning as above, we find no merit in the instant Rule and, as such, it is liable to be discharged.

22. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The assessment made in the respective Customs Nothi regarding assessment of duties and taxes of six units of Volvo Cars covered by the bill of entry as aforesaid, is declared to be lawful.

However, there shall be no order as to cost.

End.

caseno:
Writ Petition No. 4336 of 1996
With
Writ Petition No. 4337 of 1996
lawyer:
Dr. Kamal Hossain with Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, Mr. Zainul Abedin and Mr. Zakir Hossain Munshi, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner
Mr. K.S. Nabi, Attorney General ------ For Respondent No. 4 
Mr. Zakir Ahmed with Mr. Oziullah, Mr. Iqbal Ahsan Chowdhury and Mr. A.K.M. Enayet Ullah Chowdhury, Advocates ------ For Respondent No. 3
Mr. Rafiqueul Huq and Mr. M. Hafizullah, Amicus Curiae
parties:
Mostafa Kamal ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J: Since the facts as well as the points of law are identical in both the writ petitions, we heard them together and we are disposing of the two cases by one judgment.

2. In both the cases Rules were issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 23.10.96 and the impugned notification dated 18.9.96 vide Annexure-D and E respectively should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the Respondents should not be directed to levy and collect customs duty. VAT and other taxes in respect of the said imported consignment on the basis of C & F value.

3. It is stated in the application that both the petitioners opened letter of credit on 26.8.96 for import of SODA ASH LIGHT under H.S. Code No. 2836.20 at the rate of US Doller 130 per metric ton. While those goods arrived at Chittagong port, the clearing agent of the petitioners submitted bill of entry with all the relevant papers and documents for clearing of the imported goods from the vessel on 23.10.96 on payment of customs duty. VA T and other charges as the basis of C & F Value at the rate of US Doller 130 per metric ton But the office of the Respondent No. 1 on 23.10.96 directed the petitioners to declare tariff value at US Doller 220 per metric ton on the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duty and other charges in pursuance of SRO No. 2/96 Cus dated 18.9.96. It is alleged that tariff value as the aforesaid imported goods were assessed arbitrarily and as such the petitioners did not pay the customs duty on the tariff value which was fixed at US Doller 220 per metric ton. It is further submitted that tariff value would be assessed according to the value of the invoice and since the tariff value was fixed arbitrarily without considering the other circumstances the petitioners were not bound to pay the duty on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US Doller 220 per metric ton. It is further submitted that the tariff value was fixed under the provisions of section 25(7) of the Customs Act and this fixation of tariff value by notification dated 18.9.96 is absolutely arbitrary offending Articles 83.40 and 42 of the Constitution. As such the impugned notification is ultra vires of the Constitution.

4. Affidavit-in-opposition has been submitted on behalf of the Respondents. Further there are several supplementary affidavits and supplementary affidavits-in-opposition as well as reply in this case. We shall consider the papers whichever is necessary for the purpose of our judgment. It is stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioners opened L.C. on 26.3.96 and they were required to import the goods by 30.9.96. The L/C was revised on 3.10.96 and the petitioners were required to bring the goods by 30.10.96 Earlier the tariff value of such goods was fixed by notification dated 17.6.96 at U.S. Dollar 160 per metric ton. But by SRO dated 18.9.96 the tariff value was fixed at U.S. Dollar 220 per metric ton and according to this latest notification the tariff value was settled and the petitioners were required to pay duty on the basis of the tariff value fixed by notification dated 18.9.96. It is further stated that when the petitioners submitted the bill of entry with all other necessary papers, the tariff value stood 4t U.S. dollar 220 per metric ton and as such they are liable to pay the duty on the tariff value as per latest notification dated 18.9.96. In the affidavit-in-reply the petitions in fact, reiterated their statements as made in the writ petitioners. Further, some papers have been shown for importing of such goods by some other companies. Since there was discrimination in this matter, the Respondents were not authorised to fix the tariff value on the goods of the petitioners arbitrarily.

5. Before going into the merit of the case, the learned Attorney General appearing for the Respondent No. 4 has raised some preliminary objections. Learned Attorney General submits that since there was alternative remedy provided in the law itself namely, the Customs Act, the present applications are not maintainable. He further submits that already the petitioner filed applications before the Commissioner of Customs and without waiting for the result they hurriedly came before this court and obtained the present Rules. In such a situation, these writ petition are premature and the Rules are liable to be discharged. Learned Attorney General has referred to Section 193 of the Customs Act which shows the provisions of appeal as well as well the procedure for filing and disposal of the appeal.

6. Dr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that this preliminary objection cannot be entertained in view of the fad that section 193 must be read along with section 194 of the Customs Act. Section 194 of the Act shows that if duty is leviable then the entire amount of the leviable duty must be deposited first at the time of preferring the appeal and thereafter the appeal would be heard. Such a provision cannot be an efficacious remedy.
