full_judgment:
Md. Awlad Ali, J: These three references being Reference Application No. 31/99, reference Application No. 32/99 and Reference Application No. 33/99 under section 27 of the Wealth Tax Act, 1963 arise out of the judgment and order dated 3.5.99 passed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench-4, Dhaka in W.T.A. No. 26/97-98 for the assessment year 1994-95, W.T.A. No. 27/97-98 for the assessment year 1995-96 and W.T.A. No. 28/97-98 for the assessment year 1996-97.

2. The applicant for the assessment year 1994-95 filed the wealth tax return under Wealth Tax Act, 1963 showing his house property valued at Tk. 17,35,706 and Tk. 5,07,200/- the municipal annual valuation and also filed statement of assets and liabilities. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes asked the assessee applicant to file the tenancy agreement on the basis of which the house in question was let out, municipal assessment notice and the receipt showing payment of municipal tax, and accordingly the assessee produced all these papers before the Deputy Commissioner or Taxes. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes determined and estimated the value of the house property of the assessee applicant on the basis of 12th times of the gross annual rental value of the house which stood at Tk. 79,20,000/-. The applicant has stated that in the past assessment years the assessing officer determined the value at Tk. 27,29,004/-, Tk. 30,70,004/-, 32,11,879/- and 34,20,000/-, respectively. For the assessment year 1995-96 the applicant filed Wealth Tax return showing the valuation of his house property at Tk. 17,35,706/- and for the assessment year 1996-97 the applicant filed similar return showing valuation of the house at Tk. 17,35,706/- and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes estimated the value for both the years under assessment at Tk. 79,20,000/- for the purpose of imposing tax.

3. Being aggrieved by the assessment order dated 30.10.96 the assessee applicant proffered 3 appeals before the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes being Appeal Nos. 69,70 and 71/96-97 and the 3 appeals were disposed of by the said appellate Authority by order dated 30.6.97 affirming the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. The applicant then preferred second appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal being W.T.A No. 26/97-98, W.T.A No. 27/97-98 and W.T.A. No. 28/97-98. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal after hearing the parties by the impugned order maintained the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes and thereby up held the order of assessment made by the 'Deputy Commissioner of Taxes.

4. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances the applicant has referred to us the following question of law which is said to arise from the impugned judgment passed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal for our decision.

"Whether in the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in not following the statutory provision as contained in Rule-8 of the Wealth Tax Rules, 1963 and in disallowing the instant appeal and whether house property valuation could be determined at 12(times) the annual rental being such a sudden departure from the past years standard practice of gradual increase of house property valuation from Tk. 27,29,004/-, Tk. 30,70,004/- Tk. 32,11,879/- and Tk. 34,20,000/- to Tk. 79,20,000/- for the instant assessment year 1994-95."

The similar question has been formulated in other two reference applications relating to assessment years 1995-96 and 1996-97 for our answer.

5. It is contended by Mr. Ferojuddin Bhuiyan, the learned advocate for the applicant, that the Tribunal committed an error in law in not following the rule 8(3) of the Wealth Tax Rule, 1963 in determining the value of the house property of the assessee applicant. He has further contended that there are various modes of valuation for determining the value of the house property for the purpose of wealth tax and modes of valuation as envisaged in sub-rule (3) of rule 8 ought to have been applied by the Taxing authority. Mr. Bhuiyan has pointed out that rule 8(3) of the Wealth Tax Rules which was framed by the National Board of Revenue under section 46 of the Wealth Tax Act, 1963 had undergone changes from time to time and subsequently the said rule was amended by notification dated 4th May, 1982 and the proviso in the present form has been appended to sub-rule (3) of rule 8 of the Wealth Tax Rules, 1963 and the proviso as amended will although restrict the main sub-rule (3), but the assessing officer, the Deputy Commissioner of taxes, without resorting to sub-rule (3) can not estimate the value of the property equal to 12 times of the gross annual rental value of such property. It has further been pointed out by the learned Advocate that sub-rule (3) of rule 8 has again been amended and for the words twenty times the words fifteen times has been substituted by notification dated 30thJune, 1982 issued by the National board of Revenue.

6. It appears that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes being the wealth tax assessing officer determined the value of the house property of the applicant at Tk. 79,29,000/- for all the years under assessment by resorting to the proviso appended to sub-rule (3) as it now stands is in the following terms:-

"Land and buildings- The value of lands and buildings shall be estimated with due regard to the nature and size of the property, the amenities available and the price prevailing for similar assets in the same locality or the neighborhood of the said locality;

Provided that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall not except with the prior approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes, estimate a value higher than a sum equal to fifteen times the gross annual rental value of such property.

Explanation-For the purposes of this sub-rule, "gross annual rental value" means the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year."

7. The value of assets is to be determined under the Wealth Tax Act 1963 according to the provision of section 7 of the Act which is as follows:-

"Section 7 (1)-The value of any assets, other than cash for the purpose of this act shall be estimated by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes in accordance with the Rules made under section 46 of the Act. Pursuant to the provision of section 7 the rules were framed by the National Board of Revenue for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

8. Previously in sub-rule (3) of Rule 8 of the Wealth Tax Rules there were two provisos which are as follows:-

"Provided that where the capital value of such property has been determined by the appropriate local Government authority for purposes of property taxation under the laws and regulations in force in the said locality, the Wealth Tax Officer shall adopt such capital value (as determined in the latest assessment) as the value of such property for purposes of assessment to wealth tax.

Provided further that where the capital value of such property has been so determined, the Wealth Tax Officer shall not, except with the prior approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Wealth Tax, adopt a value higher than a sum equal to ten times the gross annual rental value of such property".

Before the first appellate authority the assessee 'claimed that the value should be estimated according to the municipal value as determined in the latest assessment.

These two provision have been deleted by S.R.O. No. 139-L/82 dated 4th May, 1982 and the present proviso which is stated above has been inserted with the explanation where in stead of the words "gross annual value", "gross annual rental value" has been inserted.

9. The Joint Commissioner of Taxes as it appears from the short order has upheld the order of the assessing officer without however considering the relevant provision as laid down in sub-rule (3) of rule 8 and also the power of the assessing officer to fix the valuation as provided under the proviso appended to the sub-rule. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal although has referred to sub-rule (3) and the provisos which were in force before coming into force of the amended proviso through the notification dated 4th May, 1982, but failed to apply the present provision with correct interpretation finding out the meaning and true legislative intent, and consequently wrongly upheld the order passed by the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes affirming the assessment order.

10. The cardinal principle and the mandatory provision in interpreting a section of particular statute or the rule framed there under is that the proviso controls and restricts the main section or the main rule, and proviso to a section or to a rules is to be regarded to have an overriding effect and control ever the whole section or the rule. Mr. Ferojuddin Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate, has contended that the value of the land and building for which the wealth tax is to be imposed shall be estimated firstly having regard to the nature and size of the property, the amenities  available and the price prevailing for similar assets in the same locality or the neighborhood of the said locality as per provision of sub-rule 3, but the assessing officer, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, without following the express provision as envisaged in that sub-rule estimated the value of the house property of the applicant according to the proviso which does not expressly restrict the other conditions in determining the value.

<u>11. In the proviso it is seen that the language that has been used implies that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall not estimate the value of land and building higher than a sum equal to fifteen times without the approval of the inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes. The word estimate connotes and it refers to the value to be determined with due regard to the nature and size of the property, the amenities available and the price prevailing for similar asset in the same locality or neighborhood of the said locality. In estimating the value of the property, having regard to the nature, size, amenities available and the price prevailing far similar assets in the same locality, if it does exceed the limit as mentioned in the proviso in that case approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes is necessary. In the present proviso the provision of fifteen times has been inserted only for the purpose of obtaining prior persuasion of the higher authority, namely, Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes: The proviso has not put any restriction on the power of the assessing officer to estimate the value in the manner as prescribed in the said sub-rule (3) in determining the valuation of the property and in doing so if it does exceed the sum which is equal to fifteen times the gross annual rental of such property in that case that value may he adopted for the purpose of imposing tax with the approval of the higher authority. But the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes in any case cannot follow the policy which has been incorporated in the proviso blindly and fix the sum multiplying the gross annual rental value by twelve times and fifteen times ignoring the provision of sub-rules (3). In explanation it has been stated that for the purpose of this sub-rule, gross annual rental value means .the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected the let from year to year. So this gross annual rental value is always subject to change, it may change from year to year; there is no certainty that the gross annual rental value will remain the same for all the years to come. In the instant case the applicant disclosed the yearly rental of the house at Tk. 6,60,000/- in his income tax return as bonafide annual rental and the assessing officer adopted that value and multiplied the sum by twelve times for the purpose of assessment of wealth tax, which is not permitted under sub rule (3) of rule 8 of the Wealth Tax Rules and the proviso thereof.</u>

12. In the view we are of the opinion that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was not justified at all in upholding the valuation of the house property of the assessee applicant without following sub rule 3 of Rule 8 of the Wealth Tax Rule. The question as raised is, therefore, answered in the negative and in favour of the assessee in all the 3 reference applications, But since the valuation has not been estimated according to the provision of sub rule (3) of rule 8 of the Wealth Tax Rules the matter is referred back to the Taxes Appellate Tribunal for determining the value is accordance with law and the observation made above, and in that case the Tribunal is at liberty to send the matter to the assessing officer to estimate the value in accordance with the provision of sub-rule (3).

13. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. S M Rezaul Karim, Advocate ------ for the Petitioner. 
Mr. A M. Aminuddin (A.A.G.) ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Alhaj Nazir Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The National Board of Revenue and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the fixation of value in CRF No. HKK000040, HKK 000041, HKK 000042, HKK 000043 & HKK 000044 all dated 18.3.2000 at the rate of US$ 343.40 per Metric ton and assessment made on such value shall not be declared to have been held without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to assess customs duties and taxes on the basis of invoice value at the rate of US$ 223/- per Metric ton vide invoice Nos. BP 201314-A to BP 201314-E dated 28.2.2000 and/or such other order or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. In the writ petition it has been stated, inter alia, the petitioner opened a letter of credit No. SBL.KTG/CASH/023/2000 dated 15.2.2000 for importation of 500 Metric ton of Caustic Soda Solid through Standard Bank Limited Khatungoni Branch, Chittagong at the rate of US$ 2231- per metric ton as per the invoice No. BP 201314-A to BP 201314-E dated. 28.2.2000. Before the shipment of the aforesaid goods the petitioner arranged pre-shipment inspection in China as per SRO No. 40-Lw/2000/1817/Cus dated 8.2.2000 by respondent No. 3 who issued Clean Report of Findings Certificate in short CRF Certificate Nos. HKK000040, HKK 000041, HKK 000042, HKK 000043 & HKK 000044 all dated 18.3.2000. After arrival of the cargo in the Chittagong port the petitioner through his clearing agent submitted bill of entry registration Nos. C 273344, C 25351, C 27369 dated 23.4.2000 to the customs authority for assessment of customs duties taxes and other charges. The respondent No. 2 assessed the duties and charges on the basis of the impugned CRF value with endorsement values are for customs purposes only purported to have been fixed by the respondent No.3 as per the dictation of the customs authority, as such the said value is not a CRF value in the eye of law and the same cannot be the basis for assessment of duties and charges, hence the assessment endorsed on the bill of entry dated 23.4.2000 pursuant to the impugned CRF value is also impugned in the instant writ petition. Which has been alleged illegal and is of no legal effect.

3. The learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submitted with reference to section 25A(2) of the Customs Act that in view of the provisions of law that the PSI Agency appointed under the PSI Order 1999 for verifying and certifying in the prescribed manner the price, quantity, quality and customs classification for the imports in question which shall be accepted as the basis for the assessment of customs duties, VAT and other charges and in view of the provisions of Article 5(Ka)of the Pre-shipment Inspection Order, 1999 that the PSI Agency shall endorse the price, description, quality, quantity and customs classification in the invoice and packing list and upon ascertaining its worth shall issue the certificate in accordance with law and then shall certify the CRF certificate in the prescribed manner under the provisions of Article 7(Kha) (q) of the said order maintaining the certified price as per GATT valuation agreement, the PSI agency has acted contrary to the provisions of law and Order in not verifying and certifying the price of the import on ascertaining the correctness worth of the value of the import to be the CIF value in the certificate itself inasmuch as the PSI Agency having endorsed the price of the import on the invoice and packing list as acceptable, acted contrary thereto in putting highly inflated and fictitious value as the CIF value in the certificate rendering the certificate not in accordance with law and void. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the respondent PSI Agency has failed to perform the statutory obligation ascertaining differently the CIF price of the import as contemplated under Article 7 while accepting the price appearing in the invoice and packing list and acted contrary to the provision of Jaw and the PSI Order putting inflated CIF value to be the certified price of the import inasmuch as the PSI Agency thereby surreptitiously put-ting an imaginary CRF value thereby cheating the importer which amounts to misconduct on the part of the CRF Agency. The learned Advocate has further submitted with reference to Annexure-C(1) that the petitioner having pointed out the discrepancy to the PSI Agency and not having been replied and there being violation of the law and PSI Order, 1999 and CRF Certificate not being in accordance with law and this application was maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution inasmuch as no fact need be decided but the decision could be had on the basis of interpretation of the provision of Customs Act and PSI Order, 1999 by way of judicial review by this Court.

4. The learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the respondents I and 4 taking us through the annexures and the affidavit-in-opposition has submitted that the obligation of the PSI Agency to get the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner shall be accepted as the basis for assessment but any discrepancy as to the price found in the endorsement of the invoice and in the packing list with the CIF value would not render the certificate illegal as the said CIF value was the result of ascertaining the correctness thereof, which may differ with the invoice value certified and endorsed by the PSI Agency either in invoice or packing list. The learned Deputy Attorney General with Mr. A.M. Aminuddin and Mr. M. Khaled Ahmed have however, extraneously argued that the said ascertainment of CIF value which is different from the C & F value being the basis for assessment by the customs authority, the customs authority are obliged to accept the certifying CIF value for the purpose of assessment of customs duty, vat and other charges. The learned Deputy Attorney General has further submitted that if the petitioner disagreed with the certified CIF value the importer could take recourse to Article 9 of PSI Order raising dispute firstly with the PSI Agency then with review committee then finally in an appeal both under the provisions of section 193C of the Customs Act and under the provision of Article 9 of PSI Order and in view of the specific efficacious remedy pro-vided thereunder, according to the learned Deputy Attorney General, this applications under Article 102 of the Constitution are not maintainable. Section 25A as amended on 30th June 1999 runs as under:

"25A. Pre-shipment Inspection Agencies and assessment on the basis of their certificates.

(4) For the purpose of this, Act the Government may, in the prescribed manner, appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and determine the scope and manner of their certification and related matters.

(5) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment.

(6) For the purposes of this section `price' means value of the goods determined in accordance with sub section (1) and (2) of Section 25.

5. Thus, it appears that the government shall appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and prescribe and determine the manner and the scope of their certification and related matters and that the government as well on that basis make assessment of customs duties, VAT and other charges relying on the certificate issued in the prescribed manner by the PSI agencies as to the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any imported goods duly verified and certified by the said agency and the price that has been verified and certified would be the value of the goods i.e. normal value as determined under sub-section (1) and (2) of section 25. In order to carry out the purpose of the said section to provide the prescribed manner, the government has issued Pre-shipment Order, 1999 vide SRO No. 316-Law/99/1807/Cus dated 19.10.99 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Additional Issue (Extraordinary) providing for the provision for the appointment of PSI agency and determine the scope and manner of their certification and related matters. Article 5(1)(Ka) thereof provides duties and the function on the PSI agency inter alia, as under:-

৫। (১)(ক) আমদানীকৃত পণ্যের বিবরণ, পরিমাণ, গুণগতমান, শুল্ক শ্রেণী বিন্যাস ও মূল্যের যথার্থতা যাচাই পূর্বক পণ্যের প্যাকিং লিষ্ট ও ইনভয়েস পৃষ্টাংকন (Endorce), আইন ও এই আদেশ বর্ণিত পদ্ধতি অনুসরণপূর্বক প্রত্যায়নপত্র প্রদান এবং জাহাজীকরণের পূর্বে সীল মোহরকৃত কন্টেইনারের সীল মোহরের সঠিকতা প্রত্যয়ন এবং এই আদেশে বর্ণিত অন্যান্য কার্যক্রম প্রতিপালন।

6. From the above, it is clear that the PSI agencies shall issue CRF certificate following the procedure provided in the law and in the Order upon endorsing in the packing list and invoice upon verification of ascertaining the description, quantity, quality and customs classification and price of the import and shall also ascertain the truth of the seal on the container before the shipment and other acts provided in the Order. From the above, it is thus clear that the PSI agency shall upon ascertaining the correctness of the description, quantity, quality, customs classification and price shall endorse the same in .the packing list and invoice and shall issue the CRF certificate following the procedure which been laid down under Article 7 of the order- Article 7 provides for issuance of certificate and relevant procedure, inter alia, that

“৭। প্রত্যয়ন পত্র প্রদান ও প্রাসঙ্গিক অন্যান্য বিষয়ে নিম্নবর্ণিত পদ্ধতি অনুসরন করিতে হইবে, যথাঃ-

(খ) প্রত্যয়ন পত্রে উল্লেখিত পণ্যের-

(ই) প্রত্যায়িত মূল্য GATT valuation agreement অনুযায়ী হইবে।

(ঈ) শ্রেণী বিন্যাস আইনের প্রথম সিডিউলে উল্লেখিত শ্রেণী বিন্যাস অর্থাৎ সংশ্লিষ্ট পণ্যের Heading No. এবং H.S. Code অনুযায়ী হইবে।

(গ) পরিদর্শন সংস্থা নিজস্ব লেটারহেড প্যাড পরিশিষ্ট ট্ট৭ এ বর্ণিত ফরমে প্রত্যয়ন পত্র প্রদান করিবে।

(চ) আমদানীকারক ঋণপত্র খুলিবার সময় সংস্থার নাম উল্লেখ করিবেন এবং ঋণপত্রে এই মর্মে একটি শর্ত থাকিতে হইবে যে, পণ্যের বিক্রেতা কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত প্যাকিং লিষ্ট ও ইনভয়েস পরিদর্শন সংস্থার কর্তৃক পৃষ্ঠাংকন (Endorce), কৃত হইতে হইবে এবং প্রত্যায়নপত্রের ক্রমিক নং ও তারিখ উক্ত ইনভয়েস ও প্যাকিং লিষ্টে উল্লেখ থাকিবে। ঋণপত্রের একটি কপি সংশ্লিষ্ট ব্যাংকের শাখা কর্তৃক পরিদর্শন সংস্থার স্থানীয় অফিসে প্রেরণ করিতে হইবে।

(ঞ) পরিদর্শন সংস্থা আমদানীকৃত পণ্যের সি আই এফ মূল্য প্রত্যয়নপত্রে উল্লেখ করিবে। পরিদর্শন সংস্থাকে সরকার কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত পরিদর্শন ফিস উক্ত মূল্যের অন্তর্ভূক্ত হইবে না।

7. Thus, it appears that the procedure laid down in Article 7 is that the certified price must be as per GATT valuation agreement .0 in prescribed form appendix (7) and that the letter of credit shall mention the name of PSI agency and the L/C shall contain a condition that the invoice and the packing list shall be endorsed and that the number and date of CRF certificate would be mentioned in the invoice and the packing list and the copy of the letter of credit has to be sent to the local office PSI agency by the concerned Bank. Thus, from the above, inters duty is cast upon the importer to mention name of the PSI agency in the letter of credit and the PSI agency shall also in its turn while endorsing invoice and packing list issued by the exporter shall also mention the number of certificate with date on those papers and that the PSI agency shall mention the CIF price in the CRF certificate. Article 7 provides that if it appears to PSI agency at the time of inspection that the declaration of the exporter on any subject other than the price is not justifiable and the exporter finds it difficult to meet the discrepancy or refuses to do so, then PSI agency shall issue Non-Negotiable Report of Finding (NNRF) in form in Appendix 8.

8. Article 8 of PSI order 1999 provides that if the quantity, quality, description customs classification and the price of the import has been certified and if the invoice, packing list and certificate is in accordance with law and Order, the same would be the basis for assessment. Thus, the PSI agency shall after ascertaining the correctness of the price etc, shall endorse the same in the packing list and invoice supplied by the exporter and then certify as to the CIF of the import in the CRF certificate which shall be according to the GATT valuation agreement. Clause 3 of Article 2 of the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade (GATI) provides as under;

"3. If in applying this Article, more than one transaction value of identical goods is found, the lowest such value shall be used to determine the customs value of the imported goods."

9. On perusal of the Article 5(Ka) read with Article 7(Ka) (Ga) and (Gha) of PSI Order, it is clear that prior to the endorsement or certification the PSI agency shall verify the C&F price as to its correctness/worth and if to be found in order shall endorse the same on the packing list and invoice supplied by the supplier and in case of difference it shall endorse the actual prevalent commercial price in the endorsement therein and accordingly following the procedure in Article 77 shall issue the certificate in Form (7) mentioning the corresponding CIF price (Article 7 (ঞ) which shall be according to the GATT valuation agreement.

10. On perusal of invoice of packing list it appears that PSI agency has, upon verification of the price, put an endorsement on the packing list and invoice and has accepted the same and having accepted the same the certificate must reflect the said acceptance, instead an inflated CIF price has been mentioned in CRF Certificate.

11. The PSI agency has duly verified and endorsed the invoice price as accepted value and certified to that effect on the body of the invoice and the packing list.

12. Now coming to the aforesaid provision of law the PSI agency though has a legal obligation to verify the correctness of the invoice value and to issue the certificate putting CIF price of the import in consonance thereof but in the instant cases the C&F price having been accepted on verification and endorsed accordingly in the invoice and packing list, PSI agency could not put in an imaginary amount as CIF value, which is very much inflamed and fictitious one.

13. As we already stated that there are provision for correction of the clerical error under Article 5(উ) after ascertainment of the correctness in Article 5(Ka) but the same has to be done within three days of the issuance of certificate. Admittedly, the respondent No. 3 did not provide the break up of the clarification for putting CIF value. The respondent has, however, tried to justify the CIF price by putting the CRF certificate denying any collusion as alleged between the customs authority and the CRF agency. Whether there may be collusion or not but the said respondents also could not justify that the procedure of law and order have been followed in ascertaining the correctness of the CIF value put in the CRF certificate, once having endorsed the C&F value as accepted.

<u>14. The facts and circumstances of the case go to show that the endorsement 'value for customs purpose may differ' is not contemplated under the provisions of law and Order and such arbitrary, fictitious CIF value put in CRF certificate cannot be the basis for assessment and any assessment thereon is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority. The CRF certificate with such endorsement namely, value for customs purpose may differ cannot be relied to make the certificate in accordance with law and the same would not be the price as mentioned in sub-section (3) of section 25A. Sub-section (1) and (2) of section 25 of the Customs Act authorize the department to assess normal price of the goods/import in question in the Rule considering the contemporary commercial price of the goods at the place of origin with notice to the importer or agent to produce any document or paper in support of their invoice value which shall be the basis for ascertainment of the normal price in the event of cancellation of the CRF certificate.</u>

15. Now coming to the case of the respondents we like to observe that the department has also a duty to see as to whether the PSI agency has performed their obligation in accordance with law and see the justification of the CIF value put in duly verified by the PSI agency upon ascertaining the correctness or worth of the C&F price appearing in the invoice and packing list. Such obligation has to discharged ascertaining the C&F value in the invoice and packing list and endorsing the same there of under Article 5(Ka) and 7(cha) and then put the C&F value in the CRF certificate. The department as well has a duty see that the value endorsed to be correct in the invoice and packing list by the PSI agency should tally with the CIF value in the CRF Certificate to be the basis of assessment. In case of disagreement by endorsement like value for customs purposes only differ would surely render the CRF certificate unacceptable to be the basis of assessment.

16. Now coming the maintainability of the Rule Nisi, this Court elaborately considered the issue as to maintainability in Writ Petition No. 1495 of 1996 heard together with other writ petitions disposed of on 10.4.2000 wherein in spite of alternative remedy, the rules were held to be maintainable being efficacious remedy, as the rule as to alternative remedy is not a rule of law but a rule by which this Court regulates its own proceedings and does not generally entertain any such proceeding which can be more approximately investigated in an alternative forum. General that the remedy by way of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory remedy provided under the Customs Act and referred the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. Vs. Assistant Collector of Customs, 11 BLD(AD) 227. In the case of Md. Shahidullah Vs. Collector of Customs 48 DLR (AD) 58 it was held that

"It is only when a provision of appeal in .a statute is attended with an inviolable and non-relaxable condition of payment of fine or extra duty in full that it can be said that the petitioner has no equally efficacious remedy."

17. In the case of 51 DLR 206 it has been held that "mere allegation of violation of the provisions of law cannot give rise to any cause of action for filing a writ petition when there is forum for seeking remedy against the impugned orders. Since the petitioner did not avail of the alternative forum of appeal as provided in the Customs Act and the said forum being an equally efficacious one for his remedy the rule obtained in this case should be discharged and referred the case of Delecia Diary Food Ltd. Vs. Collector of Customs 51 DLR (HC) 382 if the learned Assistant Attorney General further submitted that the petitioner is aggrieved by any order of assessment made by Collector of Customs or by Customs officer under the Collector of Customs, he is to file review and then an appeal provided under the Custom Act. In view of the above, the learned Deputy Attorney General has further submitted that the instant cases without exhausting those remedies, the petitioners cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction and referred the case of Trade Channel Vs. Collector of Customs reported in 44 DLR 127. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that where there are questions of law and interpretation of the statutory provisions remedy by way of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable and in this respect he referred the decision in the case of M/s. Usmania. Glass Sheet Factory Ltd. Vs. Sales Tax Officer, Companies Circle reported in 22 DLR (SC) 437 wherein it has been held:

"Before coming to the merits of the case it will be convenient to dispose of here the preliminary objections raised on behalf of the respondent that the writ petition was liable to be dismissed as the cause of action against the respondent was premature and the Appellant should have pursued the legal remedies provided in the Sales Tax Act- for appeal and revision to the higher authorities. Mr. Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury learned counsel for the respondent contended that the writ petition filed by the appellant was not maintainable because it was premature. According to the learned counsel no assessment has been made for the sales tax and unless it is made, the appellant has no cause of action to challenge it in the High Court. The contention of the learned counsel has not impressed it is not disputed that the appellant had to filed return of the sale of goods and under section 12(1) of the sales of the sale of goods. In the recent case, the appellant filed 14 revised Returns on the 20th of March 1965 and claimed therein that glass sheet was exempted from the payment of sales tax. On the 31st March, 1965 the Sales Tax Officer called upon the appellant to submit its explanation by the 18th April, 1965 failing which action was to be taken to realize the arrears of sales tax on the basis of Returns filed previously. The appellant submitted its explanation on the 1st April, 1965. The Central Government also agreed with the Central Board of Revenue. Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant on the 22nd, June, 1965 and called upon it to pay all the arrears of salestak within June, 1965. In my opinion, on the facts of the present case, the appellant was entitled to protect itself from the threat of the department to realize the arrears of sales tax. It is not disputed that the sales tax for the period from March 1961 to 20th of March 1965 was about RS. 4,00,000/- out of it's the appellant has failed to pay about Rs. 2,00,000/- it cannot, therefore, be said that the writ petition was pre-mature or the appellant had no cause of action against the respondent to ventilate its grievance against him. The objection of the respondent that the appellant had alternative remedies by departmental means is also not of much substance. It has been held by this Court that in a case where the dispute arises between the parties in respect of a fiscal right based upon a statutory instrument the same can be easily determined in writ jurisdiction.

In the case of Burma Oil Company (Pakistan Trading) Vs. The Trustee of the Port of Chittagong (1), it was held as under:

'We consider that since the question arose was one of fiscal right based upon a statutory instrument, it was as easily and conveniently determined in a writ petition as by means of a suit. By the exempting notification, a duty was cast upon the taxing authority viz., the Port Trustees to relive the subject against certain imposition and thereby a corresponding right to such relief was created in favour of the subject. Mandamus is in every way an appropriate remedy for the assertion of such a right by enforcement of the corresponding duty."

"To the same effect there is a decision of this Court in the case of Pakistan and another Vs.Qazi Ziauddin (2). This point was also considered in the case of Abdul Ghani and another Vs. Government of Pakistan and others (3). It was held in that case "anything done beyond or in excess of powers conferred by statute can be brought within the power of avoidance vested in the High Court. In such a case, the High Court can examine if the Officer concerned has acted in accordance with the powers conferred upon him by the statute." I would, therefore, repel the preliminary objections raised on behalf of the respondent."

In the case of Abdul Ghani and another Vs. Subedar Shoedar Khan Company and others reported in PLD 1968 (SC)131 it has been held:

"Anything done beyond or in excess of power conferred by statute can be brought within the power of avoidance vested in the High Court. In such a case the High Court can examine if the officer concerned has acted in accordance with the powers conferred upon him by the statute. If he acts within his power, section 60 will operate as a bar to the jurisdiction of the Court, but when he acts in exercise of his power, his order is susceptible in interference by the High Court in his submit jurisdiction.

" It is profitable to refer to the case of Mahboob Ali Mallik Vs. Province of West Pakistan, 15 DLR (West Pak.) 129 wherein it has been held:

"If there is no other authority which has the power to give relief of the requisite nature and extent, it is the duty of this Court in a fit case to give that relief if it has the power to do so under Article 98. There is nothing in Article 98 which would release this Court, in such a case, from that obligation, merely because it would be necessary to take evidence, whether oral or documentary, before relief could be given."

18. Thus, from the above discussion and in the facts and circumstances of the cases involved and from our decision as stated above, the respondents having not acted in accordance with law and PSI order and acted in excess of the PSI agency's power conferred under section 25A Customs Act and PSI Order, 1999 we have no hesitation to hold that the application under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute in the terms mentions in the body of the judgment directing the department to determine normal value of the goods imported by the respective petitioner in accordance with law ignoring the arbitrary and fictitious CIF value certified by the CRF agency.

The Commissioner of Customs is directed to return the Bank Guarantee and cash upon adjustment and satisfaction of their claim if any.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Alhaj Md. Nurul Huq with Mr. Choudhury Taser Ahmed, Mr. Muhammad Nazrul Islam, Mr. S.M. Zahangir Alam, Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, Ms Tania Siddiqua and Ms Chamon Akhter, Advocates ----- for the petitioners 
Mr. Md. Ozair Farooq with Mr. Sheikh Awsaful Rahman and Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, Advocates ----- for the opposite parties.
parties:
Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Abdul Jalil and others ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mozammel Hoque, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties No.1 to 40 to show cause as to why the order No.12 dated 27.7.1999 rejecting an application for rejection of the plaint passed by the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 should not be set aside.

2. Defendants are the petitioners before this Court.

3. The opposite parties No. 1 to 40 as plaintiffs instituted the instant suit for a declaration that the decree dated 23.3.1995 passed in Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 (formerly Title Suit No. 92 of 1991) is illegal and invalid and the said decree is not applicable to `Ga' schedule land. It is further prayed that the land described yin 'kha' Schedule measuring about 94 ajutangsha was purchased by the defendant No. 1 from defendants No.2 to 6. Before the trial Court the defendants filed an application under Order 7 Rule 11 read with Order 14 Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint or in the alternative for hearing the law point first. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order dated 27.7.1999 rejected the aforesaid application of the defendants.

4. Being aggrieved by the order dated 27.7.1999 the defendant petitioners preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

5. In considering the present Rule we are to consider the previous history of this case. The opposite parties No. 1 to 40 are the plaintiffs in the instant case namely, Title Suit No.42 of 1999. These opposite parties No. 1 to 40 were also plaintiffs in Title Suit No.92 of 1991 which was subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 177 of 1994. In that suit the plaintiffs (who are present opposite parties No.1 to 40) prayed for declaration of title in respect 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule land and for partitioner. In that earlier suit the present defendant-petitioners No.2 to 7 were also defendants. With regard to schedule 'ka' land in the earlier suit no dispute has arisen in the present suit. Only in respect of 'kha' schedule land of the previous suit the present suit has been filed by the self same 40 plaintiffs. In the 'kha' schedule of the plaint of the earlier suit the land of C.S. Khatian No.4300 Ja, C.S. plot No.371 was shown as 94 shatangsha and the plaintiffs' claim that out of 94 shatangsha the defendants purchased only .0090 ajutangsha by several document; in the year 1954-55. Since the defendants purchased a small portion of land by several documents in the year 1954-55, the defendants were made parties in the earlier suit as the plaintiffs prayed for d claration of title as well as partition. So, in the previous suit the plaintiffs' claim was that to defendants purchased .0090 ajutangsha land but the claim of the defendants was that the defendants purchase 9400 ajutangsha that is 94 satangsha.

6. In the earlier suit the defendants claim was that by mistake the area was written in the deed but in fact they purchased the entire suit land of C.S. plot No.371 in the year 1954 - 55 and thereafter they mutated their names and had been possessing the entire land althrough. The matter was investigated by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court and it was found by the trial Court that the defendants purchased by several documents in the year 1954-55 the entire land measuring 90 shatangsha. The plaintiffs tried to prove before the Court by showing C.S. Khatian that the said plot contained 94 decimals of land but the trial Court as well as the High Court Division found that the document of the plaintiffs namely the C.S. khatian filed by the plaintiffs was forged and fabricated. Ultimately the trial Court held that entire land measuring 90 shatangsha of C.S. plot 1lo.371 was purchased by the defendants. A portion of the land was acquired and some other portion was taken for path and ultimately .8372 acre which is 83.72 shatangsha is left and this portion was first leased out to defendant No.9 and subsequently the defendants entered into an agreement with defendant No.9 in 1989. So, the claim of the plaintiffs as well as the claim of the defendants over the present suit land was examined both by the trial Court and High Court Division in respect of area of land of C.S. plot No.371 and it was found that the defendant No.9 was possessing .8372 acre of land by virtue of agreement from the defendants. So, the trial Court dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove right, title and possession in respect of .8372 acre of land of C.S. plot No.371 and the defendants had been able to prove their right, title and possession over the aforesaid land and the defendants No. 1 to 8 in the previous suit had purchased the entire area of C.S. plot No.371.

7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court in Title Suit No.177 of 1994 the plaintiffs No.1 to 40 preferred an appeal before the High Court Division and it was registered as First Appeal No. 230 of 1995. The High Cot & Division heard both the parties and considered the matter at length. In order to prove the document of the plaintiff appellants the High Court Division took pains to call for the records from the office of the Collector and after examining the record the High Court Division found that the basic document i.e. C.S. record of rights filed by the plaintiffs was absolutely forged and concocted. In this connection, it may be mentioned that before the trial Court an Advocate Commissioner was appointed in order to measure the suit land namely, C.S. plot No. 371. From the Advocate Commissioner's report it appears that the Commissioner found .9007 acre within the boundary of the land of C.S. Plot No. 371. So, it appears that the Advocate Commissioner found more or less 90 shatangsha of land within the boundary of C.S. plot No.371. Considering the matter and perusing the record and after hearing the parties the High Court Division by a judgment and decree dated 4.3.1998 dismissed the appeal of the plaintiff - appellants and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court holding that the entire suit plot No.371 was purchased by the defendant respondents, and they have been able to prove their right, title and possession therein.

8. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the High Court Division the plaintiffs preferred a leave petition namely civil petition for leave to appeal No. 412 of 1998 before the Appellate Division. The leave petition was heard by the Full Court of the Appellate Division and thereafter the leave petition was dismissed summarily by Order dated 25.5.1998 holding that the defendants purchased vide Exts. 'ka' to 'ka (4)' .0090 acre of land of C.S. plot No.371. So, the Appellate Division dismissed the leave petition holding that the defendant purchased the entire land of the suit plot. It was further held that the certified copy of the C.S. Khatian filed by the plaintiff appellants was forged and as such the plaintiffs has no right, title as well as no particle interest in the suit plot. The plaintiff-appellants again filed a review petition before the Appellate Division vide Civil Review Petition No.45 of 1998 and the Full Court of the Appellate Division dismissed the Review Petition summarily on 5.11.1998 affirming its earlier judgment.

9. After getting decree in all the Courts as mentioned above the defendants sold .8372 acre of land to the defendant No.1 the Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. by registered Sale Deed No.3210 dated 28.7.1998. By that sale deed .8372 acre of land was sold by the defendants No.2 to 6 to defendant No. 1.

10. After sale of the above land by the defendants No.2 to 6 to the present defendant No. 1 the self same plaintiffs No. 1 to 40 again filed the present Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 with a prayer for declaring the decree passed in Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 illegal and invalid and that the defendant No. 1 had not acquired any right by purchasing the land from defendants No.2 to 6 in respect of the suit land. Though to suit land was found as 90 shatangsha, in fact after acquisition of some portion the suit land it now stands at .8372 acre which means 83.72 shatangsha. In the present suit No.42 of 1999 the self same 40 plaintiffs who were the plaintiffs in earlier suit are also plaintiffs. Defendants No. 2 to 7 were also defendants in the earlier suit and since the defendants No. 2 to 6 sold the suit land to Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. This Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. has been impleaded as defendant No. 1 in the present suit. So, it appears that the present suit land was the subject matter of the earlier suit. The present plaintiffs 40 in number are also the plaintiffs in the earlier suit and defendants No.2-7 were also defendants in the earlier suit.

11. In view of the circumstances stated above Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant petitioners, submits that in the instant suit no fresh cause of action has arisen. The cause of action according to the defendants which arose in the earlier suit had already been settled by passing a decree by the trial Court which was ultimately affirmed by the High Court Division and the Appellate Division. He further submits that the decree which was passed by the trial Court on 23.3.1995 in Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 cannot be cancelled now at the instance of the selfsame plaintiffs with regard to selfsame property in as much as the decree of the trial Court had been murged with the decree of the High Court Division and of the Appellate Division. Since the decree was affirmed by the Appellate Division it should be deemed to be a decree of the Appellate Division which cannot be set aside by the Subordinate Judge at the instance of the selfsame plaintiffs. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that the present suit is barred by law and as such provisions of Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure are very much applicable.

12. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that apart from the provisions of Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the Court can exercise its inherent power in order to settle the dispute for ends of justice. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that in the earlier suit the trial Court held that not only the plaintiffs failed to prove their right, title and possession in the suit land but also the suit was barred by limitation and this judgment and decree of the trial Court had been upheld by the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division and as such the suit is barred by law of limitation also.

13. Mr. Ozair Farooq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that he has nothing to say with regard to the decree passed in the earlier suit in view of the fact that it was up-held by the Appellate Division. But he submits that the plaintiffs claim that by several registered documents of the year 1954-55 the defendants purchased only a fraction of the suit land namely, .0090 ajutangsha which is less than a decimal. Since the defendants No. 2 to 6 sold .8372 acre of land to defendant No.1 in the year 1998. A fresh cause of action arose and that is why the plaintiffs instituted the present suit in as much as the defendants No.2 to 6 had no legal authority to sell the entire land of C.S. plot No.37I measuring .8372 acre and the defendant No.1 has not acquired any right and title by virtue of the sale deed which was executed and registered by the defendants No.2 to 6. Mr. Ozair Farooq further produce a copy of the judgment of the Appellate Division which was passed in the review petition and wanted to show that the plaintiffs claimed the disputed plot measuring .94 acre but the defendants claimed .0090 acre which is less than a decimal. So the plaintiffs had got a right to claim the remaining portion of the suit land.

14. Let us now consider the submissions of Mr. Ozair Farooq as regards the cause of action of the present suit. As we have stated above that C.S. plot No. 371 was the subject matter of the decision of the earlier suit and in that suit also the plaintiffs claimed that by several documents in the year 1954 - 55, .0090 acre of land was purchased by the defendants and not 90 decimals. Their case was that along with another C.S. plot No. 115 the defendants purchased a small fraction of C.S. plot No.371 which is less than a decimal. So, the plaintiffs till today can claim the remaining portion of the land of C.S. plot No. 371. It is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Ozair Farooq in view of the fact that the self-same claim was made by the plaintiffs in the earlier suit and on such claim they prayed for declaration of title and partition but right from the trial court up to the Appellate Division their claim was not accepted, and it was held that the defendants purchased the entire land .of C.S. plot No. 371 and the plaintiffs failed to prove the right, title and possession in respect of the said land. So, at this stage the argument advanced by Mr. Ozair Farooq cannot be accepted in view of the fact that the dispute as he is raising now in the instant suit had already been settled once for all in the earlier suit up to the Appellate Division. After getting a decree up to the Appellate Division the defendants No.2 to 6 just sold their land to the defendant No.1 Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. and by such transfer no fresh cause of action has arisen in view of the fact that the cause of action which is raising now in the instant suit had already been decided in the earlier suit by the trial Court and also by the High Court Division and the Appellate Division. As such we find that there is no cause of action for filing the instant Title Suit No. 42 of 1999.

15. In the instant Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 the first prayer was made for a declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 dated 23.3.1995 is illegal and invalid and not relating to the property which is the subject matter of the present suit. It appears to us that the decree passed by the trial Court in the earlier suit was upheld by the High Court Division and thereafter by the Appellate Division. So, the decree of the trial Court had been murged into the decree passed by the High Court Division as well as by the Appellate Division. Since the decree of the trial Court had been murged into the decree of the Appellate Division, such a decree now cannot be set aside by the trial Court in view of the fact that now it is a decree of the Appellate Division. Since the decree in the earlier suit in respect of the selfsame plot of land in between the selfsame parties had been murged into the decree of the Appellate Division such decree cannot be set aside by the trial Court again.

16. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that the suit is barred by law in view of the fact that the decree passed by the Appellate Division is the law of the land. Article 111 of our Constitution provides that the law declared by the Appellate Division shall be binding on the High Court Division and the law declared by either division of the Supreme Court shall be binding on all Courts subordinate to it. Since the judgment and decree passed in the earlier suit were affirmed by the Appellate Division, this is a law declared by our Appellate Division and as such, the present suit cannot be maintainable in view of the law declared by the Appellate Division in the judgment passed in civil petition for leave to appeal No. 412 of 1998.

17. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that in the earlier suit the trail Court passed a decree not only on merit of the suit but also on the ground of limitation and such the judgment and decree as affirmed by the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division and as such on that ground of limitation the present suit cannot be maintainable. The defendants purchased the suit land in year 1954 -55 but the plaintiffs instituted the suit in the year 1991 and on that ground the trial court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In such a situation we hold that such a suit is barred by law in view of the fact that on the ground of limitation the earlier suit was dismissed which was affirmed by the Appellate Division.

18. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that apart from the question of the Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in an appropriate case the Court can exercise its inherent jurisdiction for ends of justice. In this regard he has referred to the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. Vs. Burmah Eastern Employees Union, I8DLR(Dhaka)709. In that case Mr. Justice Murshed presiding over a Division Bench held that apart from the question of Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court can also exercise its inherent power in order to stop such exhaustive limitation added for harassing the other party again. Justice Murshed has held as follows:-

"The principles involved as two fold : in the first place, it contemplates that a still born suit should be properly buried, at its inception, so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation. Secondly, it gives plaintiff a chance to retrace his steps, at the earliest possible moment, so that, if permissible under law, he may found a properly constituted case.

Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code, as quoted above enumerates certain categories under which the Court is called upon to reject a plaint, but, it is obvious that they are not exhaustive. It appears from the language of rule 11 of Order 7 that it requires that an incompetent suit should be laid at rest at the earliest moment so that no further time is wasted over what is bound to collapse as not being permitted by law."

"Turning, now, to the plaint in the present suit, it is obvious, from a mere perusal of the plaint itself, that it must be held that the suit is prohibited under if not by law, this being the position, even if the case does not come, literally and strictly, within the letter of Order 7 Rule 11, of the Code of Civil Procedure, there cannot be any manner of doubt that the suit is prohibited under the law in the sense that it is barred under legal provisions. The Court below should, therefore, has rejected the plaint in limine because the suit itself is barred under our legal system. If Order 7 Rule 11, of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be prayed in aid, the inherent power of the Court should be invoked"

19. Mr. Ozair Farooq could not satisfy us with respect to the question of a new cause of action and that the suit is not barred by law. We have scrutinized the plaints of both the suits as well as the judgments passed by the Courts up to the Appellate Division and we are of the view that the question which Mr. Ozair Farooq is now raising had already been considered and decided in the earlier suit once for all and as such we hold that there was no cause of action for instituting the present suit. Further, we hold that since the decree passed by the trial Court in the earlier suit had already been murged into the decree of the Appellate Division such a decree cannot be challenged before the trial Court.

20. It may be mentioned that in the earlier suit dispute was raised as regards area of land sold in 1954-55 to the defendants in C.S. plot No.371. After local investigation and after considering other material evidence on record both documentary and oral, it was clearly held by the trial Court, the High Court Division and the Appellate Division that the entire area of C.S. plot No. 371 was purchased by the defendants by several registered documents in the year 1954-55. So, we hold that the plaintiffs are debarred from raising such dispute again with regard to the area of the land in C.S. plot No.371 sold to the defendants.

21. Considering the plaint of the suit and also considering the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above, we are of the view that this is a fit ease where the provisions of Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable and as such the plaint is liable to be rejected.

22. In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the impugned order dated 27.7.1999 passed in Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 is hereby set aside and the application for rejection of the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed and the plaint of Title Suit No.42 of 1999 is hereby rejected.

There will be no order as to costs.

Md Abdur Rashid, J: I have gone through the judgment prepared by my learned brother Mr. Justice Mohanunad Mozammel Haque, agreeing with him, with great respect I write out the reasons of my own for our decision to make the Rule absolute and to reject the plaint of T.S. No. 44 of 1999 of 5th Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka.

24. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge, based his decision mainly on his findings that the Supreme Court concluded that the defendants purchased 0.0090 acre only. So, claiming to have purchased 0.0090 acre only but selling 0.8372 acre showing total area of 0.90 acre to the defendant No.1 whether the defendants No.2 to 6 practised fraud or not can only he decided on evidence only the question of limitation can also be decided only after taking evidence.

25. The plaintiffs stated in paragraph 10 of their plaint as their cause of action for the instant suit that on 07.05.91 they instituted Title Suit No.92/91 (subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.177 of 1994) claiming the land in dispute measured about 0.94 acre on the other hand the defendants concealing the actual area of the suit land and practising fraud upon the court claimed the area of the suit land would be 0.0090 acre only and got the suit dismissed in the hearing of their Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal being C P No.412 of 1998 both the parties remained fire on their respective stands with regard to quantum of land of suit plot No.371. In the hearing of Civil Review Petition No.45 of 1998 also the defendants took the same stand and got the petition dismissed on 12.01.99 taking certified copy of the sale deed, the plaintiffs found that the defendant No. 2 to 6 transferred 0.8372 to defendant No. 1 admitting total area of the suit plot 371 to be 0.90 acre. The defendant No. 1 having declined to vacate possession from schedule 'Ga' land measuring 0.8282 acre which is the present suit land, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the instant suit.

26. In the aforesaid cause of action, the plaintiffs prayed for a decree for declaring (a) that the decree dated 23.03.95 passed in T. S. No. 177 of 1994 by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, at Dhaka as illegal, ineffective and not relating to the suit land.

(b) that the defendant No. 1 did not ac-quire any right title or interest in more than 0.0090 acre of the suit plot C.S. Plot 371 and also for.

(c) directing the defendant No. Ito hand over possession within 30 days of 'Ga' schedule land measuring 0.8282 acre of land in default to pass a decree entitling them to take possession through Court.

27. Mr. Nurul Haque, in support of his application under Order 7 Rule 11 and Order 14 Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, shortly the Code submitted that the suit is hit by the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, briefly the Act, barred by the decision of the Appellate Division in C.P No.412 of 1998 and also by limitation.

28. On the other hand Mr. Ozair Farooque mainly submitted that after the judgment of the Appellate Division they came to learn that the defendants No. 2 to 6 purchased only 0.0090 acre but sold 0.8372 acre. So they cannot validly convey the suit land measuring 0.8282 acre (schedule 'Ga' to the plaint) to defendant No. I as they do not have any right title or interest therein.

29. In the earlier T.S. No. 177 of 1994 the plaintiffs prayed for a decree in the preliminary form for partition of 0.94 acre of the selfsame C.S. Plot No.371 as they averred in paragraph No. 6 of the impugned plaint. But they failed to prove their right, title of possession in any part of the said land as was found by the trial court. Rather their main document exhibit 1 (Ga) certified copy of the C.S. Khatian produced by them was found to be forged upon such view, the earlier suit was dismissed. The said decree was confined both by the High Court Division and the Appellate Division.

30. Such decree being in between the same parties in respect of the self same land as the plaintiffs consistently claimed in both the suits that the total area of land in dispute is 0.94 acre is binding upon both the plaintiffs and defendants. So the plaintiffs are not entitled to such declarations as prayed for in the instant suit on the basis of decision of the earlier suit which dismissed their all sorts of claim of right title or possession in any part of the suit land in C.S. Plot No. 371.

31. The claim of the plaintiffs to institute the instant suit on new cause of action upon the decision of the Appellate Division must stand rejected outright for the decision of the Appellate Division has given a finality to the decision of the trial Court in T. S. No. 177 of 1994 that the plaintiffs failed to prove their any right title or possession in any part of the land of C.S. Plot No.371.

32. The law is now well settled that in-stances in clauses (a) to (d) of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code are not exhaustive. Even if a plaint is not barred by any law may be found to be barred under some law, namely, section 42 of the Act or section 11 of the Code etc. from reading of the plaint we are satisfied that the plaintiffs are not entitled to pray for the declarations as sought for in the suit on the basis of the decision in C.P. No.312 of 1998 of Civil Review Petition No.45 of 1998 and as such, their suit is barred under provisions of section 42 of the Act and accordingly, the instant suit is not maintainable.

33. In an appropriate case, a plaint may also be rejected even under section 151 of the Code as was held by the Appellate Division in the case of Guiness Peat (Trading) Ltd. reported in 1992 BLD (AD) 247.

"a resort to section may be made in the interest of justice in an exceptional case where the suit is foredoomed and it is allowed to be proceeded with, it will amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.

<u>34. From a reading of the plaint the fate of the instant suit becomes clear if the present suit is allowed to proceed further it would only consume the time, energy and money of all the parties concerned in such facts and circumstances of the case this court cannot allow such frivolous, vexatious and malafide suit to continue further.</u>

35. On the question of fraud, as read by the learned Subordinate Judge I must say we failed to find prima facie, any ingredients, of fraud from reading of the plaint. Mere allegation is not sufficient. To make out a case on fraud for setting aside a contested decree which was sinned up to the apex court, the plaintiffs are required to state precisely and clearly how the defendants resisted the plaintiffs from getting their cherished decree. The plaintiffs instituted the earlier suit for partition and the defendants did exactly what were expected of them to defend their interest. So, the allegation of fraud as raised in the plaint is an after thought and does not require the court to wait for the time of evidence to decide if it is permitted, then there would be no end of litigation.

36. The puzzle about the area of C.S. plot 371 surfaced around the decimal figures 0.94, 090 and 0.0090 also does not come to any help of the plaintiffs as they already failed to prove their right title or possession in any part of the suit land.

37. For the reasons stated above, in rejecting the application under Order 7 Rule 11of the Code, the learned Subordinate Judge, committed an error of law resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice and as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside and is accordingly, set aside.

End.
